contributions.text_english: Good afternoon. May I take this opportunity to welcome you back to this new term? Item 1 is questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport. Question 1, Ken Skates.
contributions.text_original: Prynhawn da. Allaf i gymryd y cyfle hwn i'ch croesawu chi nôl i'r tymor? Eitem 1 yw cwestiynau i'r Trefnydd, Prif Chwip a Gweinidog Cabinet dros Ddiwylliant a Chwaraeon. Cwestiwn 1, Ken Skates.

contributions.text_english: 1. What plans does the Cabinet Minister have to enhance support for Wales's creative industries? OQ64464
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa gynlluniau sydd gan y Gweinidog Cabinet i wella'r gefnogaeth i ddiwydiannau creadigol Cymru? OQ64464

contributions.text_english: Work is under way to deliver a new culture and sport strategy for Wales. Through the new strategy, we will recognise the creative industries as central to Wales’s cultural life, economic growth and international profile. Creative Wales will continue to support talent, skills, business growth and opportunities across Wales’s creative sectors.
contributions.text_original: Mae gwaith ar y gweill i gyflwyno strategaeth ddiwylliant a chwaraeon newydd ar gyfer Cymru. Trwy'r strategaeth newydd, byddwn yn cydnabod bod y diwydiannau creadigol yn ganolog i fywyd diwylliannol, twf economaidd a phroffil rhyngwladol Cymru. Mi fydd Cymru Greadigol yn parhau i gefnogi talent, sgiliau, twf busnes a chyfleoedd ledled sectorau creadigol Cymru.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Minister. Creative Wales has been a magnificent success, driving growth across the creative industries for a good number of years now, and, importantly, driving up the number of decent job opportunities, particularly for young creatives in Wales. As we look towards 2029, and, hopefully, the Wrexham city of culture year, we're growing the creative industries in Wrexham and across north Wales, working with a number of institutions, including the universities that we have, like Wrexham University, and we've seen the growth in the establishment of studios, including Minera Studios in Wrexham. Minister, would you agree to visit Wrexham and meet with the leaders of the creative industries within the region, and discuss what sort of support Creative Wales can offer to turbocharge the sectors in north Wales?

Minister, would you agree to visit Wrexham and meet with the leaders of the creative industries within the region, and discuss what sort of support Creative Wales can offer to turbocharge the sectors in north Wales?

contributions.text_english: Well, certainly, you have a very creative constituency. I was very pleased to be in Wrexham last Saturday for the opening—well, the reopening—of Wrexham Museum, but the opening of the football museum there, that element of it. I am going to be visiting Wrexham again soon. I have been engaging in terms of the UK City of Culture. We are all crossing our fingers, of course, in that regard, and I will be very content to engage with the Member on that. Certainly, there are very exciting things happening in Wrexham. We want exciting things to continue to happen in Wrexham, and I'm very pleased to work with any Member who represents Wrexham in order to realise that potential further.
contributions.text_original: Wel, yn sicr, mae gennych chi etholaeth greadigol dros ben. Roeddwn i'n falch iawn o fod yn Wrecsam ddydd Sadwrn diwethaf ar gyfer agoriad—wel, ailagor—Amgueddfa Wrecsam, ond agoriad yr amgueddfa bêl-droed, yr elfen yna. Dwi'n mynd i fod yn ymweld efo Wrecsam eto'n fuan. Dwi wedi bod yn ymgysylltu o ran UK City of Culture. Rydyn ni i gyd yn croesi'n bysedd, wrth gwrs, o ran hynny, ac fe fyddwn i'n hapus iawn i ymgysylltu efo'r Aelod. Yn sicr, mae yna bethau cyffrous iawn yn digwydd yn Wrecsam. Rydyn ni eisiau i bethau cyffrous barhau i ddigwydd yn Wrecsam, a dwi'n falch iawn i weithio efo unrhyw Aelod sy'n cynrychioli Wrecsam er mwyn cyflawni'r potensial hwnnw'n bellach.

contributions.text_english:
Before I begin, can I please take the opportunity to congratulate my former colleague on her latest defection yesterday? I'm sure that her newfound political beliefs and journey to the left will have her back in the Conservative Party in no time at all.

But back to the matter at hand. Minister, Julien Macdonald is a fantastic example of the talent that can come out of Merthyr Tydfil. Born and brought up in Merthyr, he went on to work with Chanel, Givenchy, and to dress some of the biggest names in the world, including Beyoncé and Jennifer Lopez. Now, sadly, his company went into liquidation in 2023, but his success was ultimately built outside of Wales due to a lack of opportunity in the Welsh creative industry and a lack of support from Welsh Governments. So, what is the Welsh Government doing to make sure that talented people from places like Merthyr Tydfil do not feel that they have to leave to build successful creative businesses? And what support can you give to help creative companies actually base themselves in Merthyr and the wider Valleys, creating jobs and opportunities? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Minister.
contributions.text_original: Weinidog.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. May I be clear? There is creativity in every corner of Wales, but, because of a lack of support previously, a lack of a strategy and a lack of clarity in terms of support from Government, that potential hasn't always been realised. What the Member will have heard in my initial response is this Government's commitment to have a real culture strategy for Wales, one that includes the creative industries, that looks at skills, that looks at opportunities for people in Wales to remain here in Wales and to be creative here. That's the difference that you will see from a Plaid Cymru Government—that we appreciate the creative industries, that we want to work with them, that we want to see them develop and also want to secure more opportunities for people to work in an area that is of great economic importance to our nation.
contributions.text_original: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Gaf i fod yn glir? Mae yna greadigrwydd ym mhob cornel o Gymru, ond, oherwydd diffyg cefnogaeth flaenorol, diffyg strategaeth a diffyg eglurder o ran cefnogaeth gan Lywodraeth, dydy'r potensial hwnnw ddim wastad wedi'i wireddu. Yr hyn y bydd yr Aelod wedi ei glywed yn fy ateb cychwynnol ydy ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth hon i gael strategaeth ddiwylliant iawn i Gymru, un sy'n cynnwys y diwydiannau creadigol, sy'n edrych ar sgiliau, sy'n edrych ar gyfleoedd i bobl yng Nghymru i aros yma yng Nghymru a bod yn greadigol. Dyna'r gwahaniaeth y gwelwch chi gan Lywodraeth Plaid Cymru—ein bod ni'n gwerthfawrogi'r diwydiannau creadigol, ein bod ni eisiau gweithio efo nhw, ein bod ni eisiau eu datblygu nhw a hefyd sicrhau mwy o gyfleoedd i bobl weithio mewn maes sydd o bwys economaidd mawr i'n cenedl ni.

contributions.text_english: Sir Fynwy Torfaen has played an important role in the music hall of fame. Rockfield Studios near Monmouth is where Queen recorded 'Bohemian Rhapsody', where Oasis recorded (What's the Story) Morning Glory?, and where the Manic Street Preachers recorded some of their most iconic music. It's also where Coldplay and the Super Furry Animals recorded at least their first albums. The list goes on. Opportunities for upcoming artists to record their music is limited, but they also need space to perform. That's why music venues like the Dragonffli in Pontypool are vital. They give music acts a stage to grow their audience and hone their talents. They've also hosted many iconic acts there as well. The business rates cut announced yesterday will make a massive difference to music venues, but how can the Government, via Creative Wales, support opportunities both to nurture new talent and ensure that music venues across my constituency and Wales can continue to produce world-class musicians and bands?

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for those points. It's lovely to hear about all those excellent things that are happening in different constituencies. Creative Wales has supported bursaries for artists and production assistants from Wales to attend Rockfield Studios workshops, opening up access to expertise in the industry while supporting local activity and strengthening the creative ecosystem more broadly. I think the point that you make is that things like this don't happen by chance. You need a strategy, you need investment, you need collaboration. What we're seeing is that there have been major bands in the past but it doesn't mean that we're definitely going to have those bands in the future. It does concern me, and I have raised this concern previously, that there are fewer young people, for example, taking GCSE drama and music, that there are fewer opportunities and courses in terms of carrying on with music, but also opportunities to perform, which are just as important. We're very lucky in Wales that we have things like Battle of the Bands when it comes to the Urdd Eisteddfod and the National Eisteddfod and so on. These provide opportunities. But certainly, as part of the long-term strategy in terms of music, we have to nurture new talent and we have to create that infrastructure. As you mentioned, the announcement yesterday will help live music venues. We need to continue to work closely with things like the Music Venue Trust in order to ensure that there is an important future for them.
contributions.text_original: Diolch i'r Aelod am y pwyntiau hynny. Mae'n hyfryd clywed am yr holl bethau gwych sy'n digwydd mewn gwahanol etholaethau. Mae Cymru Greadigol wedi cefnogi bwrsariaethau i artistiaid a chynorthwywyr cynhyrchu o Gymru i fynychu gweithdai yn Rockfield Studios, gan agor mynediad at arbenigedd y diwydiant wrth gefnogi gweithgarwch lleol a chryfhau'r ecosystem greadigol ehangach. Dwi'n credu mai'r pwynt rydych chi'n ei wneud ydy dydy pethau fel hyn ddim yn digwydd ar hap. Mae angen strategaeth, mae angen buddsoddi, mae angen cydweithio. Yr hyn rydyn ni'n ei weld ydy bod yna fandiau mawr wedi bod yn y gorffennol ond nid yw hynny'n golygu ein bod ni'n bendant yn mynd i fod â'r bandiau hynny yn y dyfodol. Mae e'n fy mhryderu i, a dwi wedi codi'r pryder yma o'r blaen, fod yna'n lai o bobl ifanc, er enghraifft, yn cymryd TGAU mewn cerddoriaeth a drama, fod yna lai o gyfleoedd a chyrsiau o ran mynd rhagddo efo cerddoriaeth, ond hefyd y cyfleoedd i berfformio, sydd yr un mor bwysig. Rydyn ni'n lwcus iawn yng Nghymru bod yna bethau fel Brwydr y Bandiau pan fo hi'n dod i Eisteddfod yr Urdd a'r Genedlaethol ac ati. Mae'r rhain yn rhoi cyfleoedd. Ond, yn sicr, fel rhan o strategaeth hirdymor o ran cerddoriaeth, mae'n rhaid i ni fod yn meithrin talent newydd a chreu y seilwaith yna. Fel rydych chi'n sôn, mae cyhoeddiad ddoe yn mynd i fod yn help o ran lleoliadau lle mae cerddoriaeth fyw yn digwydd. Mae'n rhaid i ni barhau i weithio'n agos gyda phethau fel y Music Venue Trust er mwyn sicrhau bod dyfodol pwysig iddyn nhw.

contributions.text_english: 2. What discussions has the Cabinet Minister had with sport governing bodies about safeguarding children and young people participating in grass-roots sport? OQ64436
contributions.text_original: 2. Pa drafodaethau y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'u cael gyda chyrff llywodraethu chwaraeon ynghylch diogelu plant a phobl ifanc sy'n cymryd rhan mewn chwaraeon ar lawr gwlad? OQ64436

contributions.text_english: Sport Wales, on behalf of the Welsh Government, works closely with governing bodies, clubs and community sport providers to promote robust safeguarding policies, training and procedures. The Welsh Government expects all organisations delivering sport to take safeguarding seriously, to act promptly on concerns, and to ensure that children and young people can participate safely.
contributions.text_original: Mae Chwaraeon Cymru, ar ran Llywodraeth Cymru, yn gweithio'n agos gyda chyrff llywodraethu, clybiau a darparwyr chwaraeon cymunedol i hyrwyddo polisïau, hyfforddiant a gweithdrefnau diogelu cadarn. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn disgwyl i'r holl gyrff llywodraethu chwaraeon gymryd diogelu o ddifrif, gweithredu'n brydlon ar bryderon, a sicrhau bod plant a phobl ifanc yn gallu cymryd rhan yn ddiogel.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Minister. Volunteer coaches and committee members in communities across north Wales, including Flintshire and Wrexham, give up their evenings and weekends to give our young people fantastic opportunities. I know this because I've been involved in grass-roots sport for a long time. Yet they are increasingly drowning in red tape while struggling to access timely safeguarding training and DBS checks. What concrete practical support and funding is your department providing directly to grass-roots clubs to ensure robust safeguarding does not become an insurmountable administrative barrier that forces local clubs to close? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Welsh Government has been working together with other Governments across the United Kingdom. There was a 'Safe Sport Project Report' that was published in 2025. This was commissioned after intensive engagement with governing bodies, sport councils, athletes and people who have lived experience. Sport Wales represents Wales in terms of that work. In our first intergovernmental meeting as sport Ministers from all parts of the United Kingdom, we discussed this in Glasgow during the Commonwealth Games. This is an important issue. It is an issue that is not just relevant to Wales. Obviously, I will make sure that that work goes forward. Of course, if any Member is aware of any concerns, then we all have a responsibility to report on that and I would encourage anyone to make sure that that happens.
contributions.text_original: Mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi bod yn cydweithio efo Llywodraethau eraill ledled y Deyrnas Unedig. Roedd yna adroddiad prosiect ar chwaraeon diogel a gyhoeddwyd yn 2025. Comisiynwyd hwn ar ôl ymgynghoriad helaeth efo cyrff llywodraethu, cynghorau chwaraeon, athletwyr a phobl sydd â phrofiad byw. Chwaraeon Cymru sy'n cynrychioli Cymru o ran y gwaith hwn. Mi wnes i, yn fy nghyfarfod rhynglywodraethol cyntaf efo Gweinidogion chwaraeon eraill y Deyrnas Unedig, drafod hyn yn Glasgow yng Ngemau'r Gymanwlad. Mae hwn yn fater o bwys. Mae o'n fater sydd ddim dim ond yn berthnasol i Gymru. Yn amlwg, fe fyddaf yn sicrhau bod y gwaith hwnnw'n mynd rhagddo. Wrth gwrs, os oes yna unrhyw Aelod yn ymwybodol o le mae yna bryderon, mae'n ddyletswydd arnom i gyd fod yn adrodd ar hynny ac mi fyddwn i yn annog unrhyw un i sicrhau hynny.

contributions.text_english: Like Nigel and many parents across Wales, I spend much of my weekends on sidelines across my constituency, and I want to give a heartfelt thanks to all of our dedicated coaches across Wales, because grass-roots sport wouldn't exist without those hard-working volunteers. Sport clubs must be an environment where young people build friendships and they improve their mental and physical well-being. Young women in particular are more likely to become leaders when they participate in team sport. But too many young people are prevented from accessing these clubs because of the associated costs: kit, boots, fees, even getting to games. So, Cabinet Minister, I'd like to ask how you will ensure that governing bodies promote accessible pathways to participation so that every child can access the lifelong benefits of grass-roots sport.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for raising those important points. Central to the whole vision of this Government in relation to sport and culture is ensuring participation for all without barriers. That is part of our call for evidence at the moment, which will be open until the 18 December, so please encourage people to present evidence to that because we know that barriers exist. You've mentioned some of them, but there are others too. If we want everyone to have those opportunities, then, I agree with the Member, we must take action. So, I very much hope that, coming out of the new culture and sports strategy, ensuring participation for all will be a central part of the strategy, and I will be working with other Ministers, including the Minister for education and the Minister for social justice too.
contributions.text_original: Diolch am godi'r pwyntiau pwysig hynny. Yn ganolog i holl weledigaeth y Llywodraeth hon, o ran chwaraeon a diwylliant, mae sicrhau cyfranogiad i bawb a dim rhwystrau. Mae hwnna'n rhan o'n galwad ni am dystiolaeth ar y funud, sydd ar agor tan 19 Rhagfyr, felly plîs a wnaiff pawb annog pobl i gyflwyno tystiolaeth, oherwydd rydyn ni'n gwybod bod yna rhwystrau'n bodoli ar y funud. Rydych chi wedi crybwyll rhai ohonyn nhw, ond mae yna eraill. Os ydym ni eisiau i bawb gael y cyfleodd hynny, yna, dwi yn cytuno efo'r Aelod, mae'n rhaid gweithredu. Felly, dwi'n mawr obeithio, yn dod allan o'r strategaeth ddiwylliant a chwaraeon newydd yma, y bydd sicrhau cyfranogiad i bawb yn rhan ganolog o hynny, a chydweithio efo Gweinidogion eraill, gan gynnwys y Gweinidog addysg a'r Gweinidog dros gyfiawnder cymdeithasol hefyd.

contributions.text_english: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. The Reform UK spokesperson, Louise Emery.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf y nawr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Louise Emery.

contributions.text_english: Cabinet Minister, thank you for coming to the culture committee on Monday, where we discussed the shadow broadcasting and communications authority for Wales. I'd like to press you further on this, if I may. You referred in committee to the 2023 expert panel report as evidence for supporting your approach to this shadow authority. As a lot of us weren't there in 2023, I thought I'd just remind us of the remit of that panel. The main purpose was to provide options and recommendations on the delivery of the Welsh Government and Plaid Cymru co-operation agreement at the time to explore the creation of this shadow authority. The panel will have specific regard to that and will be expected to build on that initial thinking within the co-operation agreement. So, it may well have been an expert panel, but I'm not sure it was independent advice given. So, I'd like to ask the Minister what independent assessment your Government has undertaken of the alternative—that the problems identified by the panel, which we both agree on, could be addressed within the existing UK regulatory framework without any need for a shadow authority.
contributions.text_original: Cabinet Minister, thank you for coming to the culture committee on Monday, where we discussed the shadow broadcasting and communications authority for Wales. I'd like to press you further on this, if I may. You referred in committee to the 2023 expert panel report as evidence for supporting your approach to this shadow authority. As a lot of us weren't there in 2023, I thought I'd just remind us of the remit of that panel. The main purpose was to provide options and recommendations on the delivery of the Welsh Government and Plaid Cymru co-operation agreement at the time to explore the creation of this shadow authority. The panel will have specific regard to that and will be expected to build on that initial thinking within the co-operation agreement. So, it may well have been an expert panel, but I'm not sure it was independent advice given. So, I'd like to ask the Minister what independent assessment your Government has undertaken of the alternative—that the problems identified by the panel, which we both agree on, could be addressed within the existing UK regulatory framework without any need for a shadow authority.

contributions.text_english:
I don't know if my officials have had an opportunity to share with the committee yet the range of evidence that I referred to during my question session with the committee. I referred to the IWA report, the Institute of Welsh Affairs, which was independent and was not commissioned by Government. I referred to academic research that was also not commissioned by Government. There is a broad range of evidence out there. The work done in terms of the co-operation agreement emerged from that.

I would also encourage Members to look at the work done during the fifth Senedd by the committee that you're now a member of, which, on a cross-party basis, not from Government, was scrutiny work carried out by previous Members of this Senedd that confirmed that broadcasting isn't working for Wales as it currently stands, and encouraged Government to take action. So, what I'm doing as a Minister is acting on independent recommendations—listening and acting—and that's what I hope that any Minister would do in my position.
contributions.text_original:
Dwi ddim yn gwybod os ydy fy swyddogion i wedi cael cyfle i rannu gyda'r pwyllgor eto yr ystod o dystiolaeth roeddwn i'n cyfeirio ato fo yn ystod fy sesiwn ateb cwestiynau. Mi wnes i gyfeirio at adroddiad yr IWA, yr Institute of Welsh Affairs, a oedd yn annibynnol a ddim wedi'i gomisiynu gan Lywodraeth. Mi wnes i gyfeirio at ymchwil academaidd sydd hefyd ddim wedi'i gomisiynu gan Lywodraeth. Mae yna ystod o dystiolaeth eang yma. Mi oedd y gwaith a wnaed o ran y cytundeb cydweithio yn deillio o hynny.

Mi fyddwn i hefyd yn annog Aelodau i edrych ar waith a wnaed yn ystod y pumed Senedd gan y pwyllgor rydych chi rŵan yn aelod ohono fo a ddangosodd yn drawsbleidiol, ddim gan y Llywodraeth—. Roedd yn waith craffu gan Aelodau blaenorol o'r Senedd hon a oedd yn cadarnhau nad yw darlledu yn gweithio i Gymru fel ag y mae o ac yn annog bod angen i'r Llywodraeth weithredu. Felly, yr hyn dwi'n ei wneud fel Gweinidog ydy gweithredu ar argymhellion annibynnol—yn gweithredu a gwrando—a dyna dwi'n gobeithio buasai unrhyw Weinidog yn ei wneud yn fy sefyllfa i.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for that answer, and, as I think we agree, nobody disputes that journalism faces financial pressures, particularly in Wales, that viewing habits are changing and that Welsh language broadcasting should definitely be supported. And I refer to the Welsh Affairs Committee, which heard evidence from S4C in the last week or so, working successfully with the BBC, Ofcom and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to improve the prominence of Welsh language content and address these problems. None of these discussions stated that devolution was the best outcome. Referring to our committee discussion, we talked about the need for funding for extra journalists particularly. So, do you believe that, if this goes ahead as, obviously, a shadow authority, ultimately devolving broadcasting powers to Cardiff would actually mean funding available to solve these problems, and where would this money come from? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I believe, and I would hope that every Member would agree, that we in Wales should have a voice and that decisions on Wales should be made in Wales. The fact that we don't have a voice as a Government in relation to what's happening in terms of the BBC charter at the moment, that we are consulted with just as any individual in Wales would be, and that we don't have a voice, really is unjust—that the future of S4C is reliant on decisions being taken in a Parliament that isn't here in Wales, without any need to take into account your views in terms of scrutiny, or my views as a Minister. I'm sure you'll join me in congratulating our athletes and coaches on their achievements and the pride they have brought here to Wales. Given the success of these major sporting events, and the benefits that they bring in terms of participation, economic investment and international profile, can you tell us what the Welsh Government is doing to attract major sporting events to Wales?

contributions.text_english:
I certainly agree with you. I was very proud of Team Wales, and not just those that won the medals; there were some wonderful and excellent performances, and we should be extremely proud of the whole team. As I mentioned in my appearance before the committee, when I was in Glasgow, to see that Wales had made such am impression, that they were everyone's second favourite team for everyone who wasn't from Wales, was wonderful to see. Clearly, there was some very sad news over the summer too, and I would like to take this opportunity to mention Fin Tarling. Our thoughts are with his friends and family. That was a disastrous occurrence over the summer.

In terms of our strategy now, I do want to ensure, in terms of major events—. I was very pleased yesterday that we saw that the UEFA Women's Champions League was to come to Wales in 2029. I'm pleased to say that that was one of my decisions as a Minister to support that, and that shows that we are taking action. But I have been very clear, too, that all major events that we bid for have to be for a purpose and that we will have considered, before making a bid, what the investment would be, but also what the value will be economically, socially, and outcomes in relation to that.

You and I have been here in the past and have seen Governments perhaps failing to outline what success looks like, and that is certainly something that I'm looking at now in relation to the Tour de France and also the 2028 Euros. But those measures and yardsticks should be in place before we bid, and we should have an idea of what we want to achieve. So, we are reviewing the major events strategy, and I will be taking that work forward. The work has commenced, but we will take it further.

I'm glad that the Member referenced the work that we've prioritised in terms of understanding the need, because the thing that I'm determined to do is have a plan in place long term, because, as I said in evidence to the committee, we do know, in some sectors, the investments needed, and the figures are eye-watering. They're not the kind of finances that we have currently available, they're nowhere near enough what's needed, and we will need to look strategically once we know that full picture.

I completely agree with you—and I think I mentioned this in my response to Mike Hedges during committee on Monday, when he asked me about bidding for the Commonwealth Games—we can't just invest in facilities to attract major events if then it means there's no money left to invest in key infrastructure like our swimming pools, like 3G pitches and so on, and that means that people in your constituency, in other constituencies across Wales, then fail to have access. So, this work will then be able to outline what investment is needed, where public investment is needed, how we work with local authorities, work with different budgets, because there are investments made in schools, for instance, in sport facilities.

The guarantee I give you is that we will have that long-term strategic approach, working with national governing bodies, Sport Wales, working with local authorities, working across portfolios, to ensure that we identify where the gaps are, where infrastructure is at point of failure as well, because we know a number of swimming pools are extremely old across Wales and are at risk of not being financially viable or able to stay open. We know some have closed already. That's my commitment. We want to see the right facilities that people will be able to use so they can stay active, be active in their communities, and that means every corner of Wales, rural Wales, including urban.

Grass-roots clubs should be at the heart of the Welsh Rugby Union's decision making. The decision to drop either the Ospreys or the Scarlets will be devastating for communities across south-west Wales. As someone from Ystradgynlais, for example, I would say that, if you were to tell me that there was no longer to be a local derby between Ystradgynlais and Ystalyfera, there might be some form of civil disorder, even. This is a decision of much graver consequences, as it used to be said, in the Swansea valley at least, that there were two places of worship for the Welsh people and it was debatable whether it was chapel or the rugby pitch that was the most culturally significant.

The Ospreys' and Scarlets' success is known across Europe, with both teams also heavily contributing to Wales's international success. The people demand, rightfully, and deserve transparent answers, as you say, from the Welsh Rugby Union, which they've not been given. As we've seen too frequently in south Wales, when industry leaves—and this is a form of industry—nothing takes its place. Does the Minister agree that the Welsh Rugby Union should provide the transparency, accountability and collaboration on how they got to their decision to drop either the Ospreys or the Scarlets? Thank you.

I'd like to start by saying thank you to the Member for raising the question, and apologise because I think it's in the same vein. But Minister, the Welsh Rugby Union recently wrote to me and told me why it is cutting four professional clubs to three. What it has not told me in that letter is why the metric used differs from one part of Wales to another.

In the east and the capital, geography settled it, quite clearly. Cardiff and Newport were each given their own licence area, and the incumbents were confirmed. No competition, no scoring, no test of merit. The WRU's own letter to me confirms that the factors weighted most heavily there were population, accessibility and infrastructure. Performance and pathways came second. So, in summary, geography decided two of the licences, and merit was only demanded in determining the third spot. The most damning indictment of this decision in that correspondence is that the two clubs already chosen are our worst performing with regard to silverware, and the two being asked to fight out the remaining spot, the Scarlets and the Ospreys, are the two most successful clubs in the modern Welsh rugby era.

If, as the WRU state, the intention of this exercise is to ensure that Welsh rugby is once again a force in the game at regional and international levels, then it is quite at odds with the fact that the two clubs being asked to determine their eligibility for the third spot have produced more internationals than either Cardiff or Newport. So, will the Cabinet Secretary join me in calling for the WRU to finally publish the evidence and the scoring decisions that have brought us to this stage?

contributions.text_english: 4. What is the Welsh Government doing to support the development of a professional rugby team in north Wales? OQ64432
contributions.text_original: 4. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i gefnogi datblygiad tîm rygbi proffesiynol yng ngogledd Cymru? OQ64432

contributions.text_english: As I've already outlined this afternoon, the WRU is the independent governing body for rugby in Wales and is responsible for decisions about the structure and development of the professional game, including in north Wales. The Welsh Government does not fund professional sports teams, but through Sport Wales we support the community and the grass-roots game.
contributions.text_original: Fel dwi wedi amlinellu eisoes heddiw, mae Undeb Rygbi Cymru yn gorff llywodraethu annibynnol ar gyfer rygbi yng Nghymru ac mae'n gyfrifol am benderfyniadau ynghylch strwythur a datblygiad y gêm broffesiynol, gan gynnwys yng ngogledd Cymru. Nid yw Llywodraeth Cymru yn ariannu timau chwaraeon proffesiynol, ond trwy Chwaraeon Cymru rydyn ni yn cefnogi'r gymuned a'r gêm ar lawr gwlad.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. A hundred and twenty-one million people worldwide watched the 2023 six nations championship across 209 international territories. Six nations matches regularly attract UK television audiences of up to 4.5 million viewers. Welsh rugby generates an estimated £225 million to £250 million annually through the professional game and match-day activity. An independent study commissioned by the Welsh Rugby Union found that Principality Stadium contributes £2.75 billion in economic output and supported around 2,500 jobs annually. 

Now, despite this, there does remain a clear imbalance in the professional game. Professional men's rugby has long been concentrated in Cardiff, Swansea, Llanelli and Newport, leaving north Wales without a professional regional team. As the WRU moves towards a three-region model, there are concerns that opportunities for supporters and talented young players in north Wales could be further diminished. How exactly are you going to redress this inequality?

Thank you to the Minister for her answers so far and to Janet for bringing this question forward. Minister, when I look across my constituency, I see a wealth of great rugby clubs, whether that's Colwyn Bay, Denbigh, Mold, Ruthin, Rhyl, to name just some. Their squads, staff and supporters show every week the important role that rugby plays across Clwyd and across Wales. However, when speaking to these teams and others, I'm told that young talent is often scouted and drawn across into English rugby pathways. contributions.text_english: Thanks very much indeed. Communities across Wales's participation in grass-roots rugby is not only beneficial to players but gives a vital outlet for socialisation and channels investment into local economies, which is particularly important. contributions.text_english:
You raise an extremely important point, and I don't have the powers to intervene in that manner, but what I am doing at the moment, through the work that we are doing, is to understand what the situation actually is in terms of libraries the length and breadth of Wales. They're a statutory service. We know that there have been cuts across Wales. Many Members here will have campaigned to retain their local libraries, and I am deeply concerned about the future of our libraries—the future in terms of that investment.

We need to understand what the situation is, and that is why, in terms of a long-term vision and strategy and to be clear on the long-term investment needed, I can give an assurance to the Member that I do believe that libraries are important, that this work is ongoing, and that we would want to work with local authorities, certainly, in order to ensure that the right services exist in our communities and that there is access to our libraries.

Thank you. Trefnydd, the Government is committed to the decolonisation of Welsh history, but this represents an attack on Welsh identity. The British empire was ultimately a force for good in the world, and the Welsh played an important role in bringing technology, education, common law, democracy, and Christian ideals, such as the primacy of truth and the dignity of individual human life, to peoples and cultures with no such previous concepts. Indeed, without British colonisation, the institution of slavery would have continued across the globe unabated. Rather than decolonising history, we should just tell it honestly, and that would mean conceding that, during the period of colonisation, the conscience of the British empire was the most morally sophisticated the world has ever known.

Trefnydd, will you agree that using contemporary moral standards to judge the empire that actually had to formulate those moral standards first-hand, because they didn't exist previously, is not only bad historical practice, it shows immense ingratitude to those who gave us the ideas that we now take for granted?

contributions.text_english: 1. What lessons has the Cabinet Minister learnt since failing to pass the first supplementary budget for 2026-27, and how will this inform the Welsh Government's approach to future budgets? OQ64442
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa wersi y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'u dysgu ers methu â phasio'r gyllideb atodol gyntaf ar gyfer 2026-27, a sut y bydd hyn yn llywio dull gweithredu Llywodraeth Cymru o ran cyllidebau yn y dyfodol? OQ64442

contributions.text_english:
There are lessons for Government and political parties from the supplementary budget vote. In a Senedd with no overall majority, co-operation and responsible decision making are essential as we look forward to future budgets. The Government wants to engage constructively across the Senedd to ensure that budgets are a blend, as I see it, of three component parts: funding for the delivery of effective public services, funding for priorities brought into Government by Plaid Cymru, and funding for other priorities from other political parties.

In order to produce a blended budget that can command a Senedd majority, my only plea across the Chamber is that we have a common understanding also of the financial envelope available to us. We are facing the most challenging budget settlement of this decade in 2027-28, with a real-terms reduction of around 0.7 per cent in resource funding, and even greater reductions in capital budgets. The financial envelope for next year's budget is especially tight, and will require a particular discipline for this Government and for all of us who want to play a constructive part in passing Wales's annual budget.

I'm not sure whether I will always welcome a question from Andrew R.T. Davies as Cabinet Minister for Finance, but today in particular, it was particularly useful for me to see that your question, constructed in this manner, allowed me to outline some of my thoughts on how I see the future of budget discussions. And, yes, we are keen, as the First Minister has said, to have discussions with all political parties. We are very conscious of the fact that we are a minority Government. If that supplementary budget vote was useful in anything, it was useful in reminding us, as a Government, that we need to command a majority to pass any budget in this place.

So, I look to all Members here to consider our roles in a different way perhaps to how we have considered our roles and participation in budgets of the past. In fact, the Welsh Conservatives have an advantage over all other political parties here. You're almost the continuity party in this Senedd, because you are an opposition party and you've played—[Interruption.] You're consistently an opposition party; I do not prejudge the future. But Reform is a new party in this Senedd, Labour is a party in opposition for the first time and Plaid Cymru is a party in Government, and there are new roles for all of us to play in that. But I hope that as we continue discussions over the next few weeks and months—. And those discussions are happening, and I want now to use pace and to think about how we can have those discussions across political parties and individuals in this Chamber to bring ideas into this big melting pot that is the annual budget. So, I hope that we can do that in a more meaningful way than we have done coming out of the election before the summer. And I think that's a challenge that all of us have to rise to, and me, in particular, as the finance Minister.

contributions.text_english: One of the most common things I've heard since being elected is the difficulties the public sector and third sector are facing with short-term and single-year funding. It's clear that throwing money at an issue isn't going to solve the root cause of it, and, for a long time, it felt like that was the case. After 26 years of the previous Labour administration, as we know, one in three children are still living in poverty, our waiting lists are at their highest and there's been little behavioural change in walking and cycling rates, despite the promotion of active travel—all issues that we've inherited from Labour. So, does the Cabinet Minister agree that genuine, lasting change is more likely to be delivered through long-term, sustainable funding, with clear accountability for results?

contributions.text_english: Cabinet Minister, yesterday's announcement of a 30 per cent cut in business rates for some of the smallest hospitality accommodation and leisure venues is certainly a welcome step forward. However, there is plenty more that the Welsh Government can do to support the tourism industry in Ceredigion Penfro, including reducing the devastating 182-day occupancy threshold for self-catering businesses. Now, I appreciate that the Welsh Government's consulting on this, but the consultation states that there will be a limit to the extent of any reduction in the threshold, arguing that a substantial decrease in the threshold could incentivise an oversupply of self-catering properties. In light of this, can you clarify what the Welsh Government considers to be the minimum viable occupancy threshold? And in the interests of transparency, will you commit to publishing the evidence underpinning that position, so that business owners can understand the parameters that the Welsh Government is considering in this important consultation?

Well, it's always been something that's been a topic of debate in this Senedd, and within Plaid Cymru too, in terms of what is that point where you're striking the balance in the housing market between the housing stock available for people to live in and also the housing stock available for the tourism and self-catering sector, and striking that balance, so that one doesn't have a negative impact on the other, getting that balance right, is important. And that is what we hope to deliver through consulting on this.

I've already had discussions with representatives of the self-catering sector, who, clearly, do believe that the balance is at a lower point than the 152 days in the consultation, and you perhaps feel the same. Now, I am open to having that discussion. I sense that the response to the consultation will demonstrate that the sector itself, and those within the sector, do believe that we need to go deeper than what's contained within the consultation, but the Government does want to strike the right balance. We don't want to create further problems for ourselves by setting this threshold too low. But I am eager that we reach a position where this system that impacts our housing sector, but also our self-catering and tourism sectors, reaches a point where it can be a permanent solution in this area. So, I'm open to discuss this with you too in terms of how we get the outcome to this consultation to reach a point that has majority support in this place.

contributions.text_english: Minister, what financial support will you prioritise to attract visitors to Ceredigion and Pembrokeshire outside of the summer months, so that tourism can sustain year-round jobs and give young people greater opportunities to work locally?
contributions.text_original: Minister, what financial support will you prioritise to attract visitors to Ceredigion and Pembrokeshire outside of the summer months, so that tourism can sustain year-round jobs and give young people greater opportunities to work locally?

contributions.text_english: A year-round tourism economy is something that I definitely want to see, both for the constituency that we both represent, but also for Wales generally. I think we've seen significant progress on that over the last few years, but there is more to do still on that. We have our investment priorities, and looking at how we can attract tourists for an extended period of the year is part of the criteria in how we invest in that. Also, we need to make sure that the business rates system that we have, and other taxation aspects, are also ensuring that those businesses that support the hospitality sector are able to be all year round. There's no point having businesses that are only open for a particular part of the year. We need businesses that are open all year long, so that they can provide the opportunity for tourists to benefit, but also, what benefits tourists also benefits the communities they serve. So, I'm particularly hopeful that the positive sign that the Government was able to give yesterday for such a wide array of businesses that do support the tourism sector, of a 30 per cent reduction in business rates from next April, is a positive sign for the tourism sector generally that this Government backs it.

contributions.text_english: There are two aspects to this; I've spoken, actually, twice on the politics show on both of them. One was the in-year challenges that the Welsh Government inherited as a result of the budget that was laid last year and passed last year. The pressures in particular from within the NHS are considerable, and they were considerably more than I expected them to be. They are a challenge within the financial year that I'm trying to manage as we speak. So, those were two aspects that were particularly challenging for public services in Wales.

contributions.text_english:
It was fully costed, but the job of work that we have to do as a Government, and I've alluded to it already, is the discipline now that Ministers have to face in allocating within their priorities how they marry the priorities that a governing party brings into Government with the day-to-day running of public services. 

I spoke of the three components of the budget as I see them: the effective running of public services in Wales and how we fund those in the budget settlement that we have as a Senedd and Government; and then the priorities that the Plaid Cymru Government, as voted for by the people of Wales, bring into that; as well as then, of course, the ability that other political parties will want to influence that budget as a third component part of it. So, putting all of that together in one blended melting pot is what we're doing as we speak. Doing that at a time of more financial flexibility would have made it an easier and more constructive piece of work to undertake. It is going to be a challenging piece of work. As I've hopefully set out today, I hope that we're all up for that challenge as a Senedd together.

Well, thank you for your response, Cabinet Minister. France Limited, a significant amount of taxpayers' money. contributions.text_english: Thank you very much for that, Cabinet Minister. Thank you for the supplementary question, and I'm sure it must have been a terrible summer for those farmers and commoners in your area and elsewhere in Wales where they faced these fires with very real consequences on how they did their farming and livestock farming. 

I have had discussions, and they continue, with the rural resilience Minister about the financial implications of both the direct fires and also such a difficult summer in terms of harvest and growing that the drought led to here in Wales. So, we'll continue those discussions. I'll discuss that particular letter with him as well.

But also, to the point you make about the longer term implications of what we face as a country, as a world, in terms of the different challenges that have really struck home this year, I think, in a way, that we've seen bits of it in the past, over the past few years where we've had some intense periods of heat and wildfire consequences, but we've never seen it in such a sustained way over such a long period of time. And so, this asks questions of our sustainable farming scheme. Of course, we've made the long-term financial commitment, multi-year, of £1 billion on that scheme, but we do need to look at the content of that scheme, going forward, in order to meet some of the challenges that were discussed yesterday, actually, in this Senedd over how we manage our uplands and mountain areas in particular.

contributions.text_english: Minister, a fortnight ago, I attended the defence security and resilience conference in Newport, something rather naively described by opponents as an arms fair. It wasn't an arms fair. Resilience was a really key part of it, and some of these discussions we've had featured there highly in terms of flooding and wildfires. The First Minister yesterday quite rightly referred to resilience several times in his statement regarding the wildfires, and, indeed, we have a Cabinet member that has that word in the description. So, my question is, really: looking as to when these events occur in the future, and we do need to build into our land management more resilience—things like firebreaks and ponds, and so on—is the Minister prepared to talk about the financial impacts of the sustainable farming scheme, in particular, in terms of working into that scheme how we can build more resilience into our system so that we can prevent the extent of these fires in future?

Yes, I agree, and I'm sure this summer has brought it home to the Minister, just as much as it has to farmers, how we manage land. Farmers knew this already, by the way. They were telling Ministers, I think, over the years about how some of the changes in support schemes are having effects on our uplands. But this year has brought to the forefront how there is a very direct relationship with how we farm our uplands and what happens in those uplands, both in terms of wildlife and regeneration of wildlife, but also in how we manage the uplands both in order to prevent floods downstream and also to ensure that we have adequate measures for limiting wildfires in these excessive heat situations that we have.

We are facing and we are likely to have to plan for these events to become possibly even annual events. We know that our climate is changing, and we as a Government and as a Senedd need to own up to that fact and to take the measures that we need to in order to make Wales resilient in the nature of the climate change that we are seeing in our society.

contributions.text_english: Within the Welsh Government, responsibility for local government lies with my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning, but we are aware across the Government that there is financial pressure on local authorities as they deliver important public services.

contributions.text_english: Diolch. Cabinet Minister, councils across Wales are at breaking point. Council tax rises this year have already added around £104 on average to band D bills across Powys, Neath Port Talbot and indeed Swansea, yet people are still paying more whilst roads crumble and front-line services disappear too. And now we are losing our primary schools. Cradoc primary school, for instance, in a nearby village to me, has already closed. When a primary school is closed, it's ripping out the heart of our communities. And clearly, under this Plaid Government, more school closures are coming too. My main question is this: as you have now commissioned a review of the funding formula, including rurality and sparsity, will you now admit that the current system is failing, and will you guarantee fairer funding, so taxpayers aren't continually asked to pay more for less, while our communities lose their services and more children lose their primary schools too? Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I represent a rural community, and have done over the years, so I'm very familiar with the fact that there are many factors that are at play in designing and deciding on the future of rural schools. It is not just the availability of public funding. Rural communities and aspects within those rural communities are a challenge, especially when we think about the depopulation, especially of our younger population, from many of our rural communities. How we look across Government as to how we can support that, not just in terms of money, but in how we are designing support, housing and economic opportunity for our rural areas, is important.

The important piece of work that this Government has started, though, is how we design a local government formula that meets the complexity of needs that our local authorities have. You rightly identified two of them in rurality and sparsity and the difficulty and expensive nature of delivering services across rural and sparse areas. We had reference made earlier to other priorities as well in terms of socioeconomic deprivation. Making sure that we strike a better balance in how we can deliver services effectively to all our communities in Wales is the journey that this Government has commenced in this piece of work, and hopefully all of us can involve ourselves in that.

contributions.text_english: The outlook for the Welsh budget remains extremely challenging. The expectation is that resource funding will fall 0.7 per cent in real terms in 2027-28 and that capital budgets will decline over the next three years, in contrast to the average real-terms growth of 3.5 per cent per year seen since the start of the decade.

contributions.text_english: It's always interesting when you decide where you want to start something, because if you started in 2011, you'd have seen an entirely different figure. contributions.text_english:
I don't dispute the Holtham commission. I don't dispute the point you made at the start that wherever you start your analysis of any data, you can assess that. I'm trying to think of how we think about public service delivery now in the post-COVID period. That's why I was identifying this decade only. But you and I were in Senedds of the past where those austerity years of public finance in Wales, under a different political regime at a UK level, were particularly difficult at that time as well. So, I'm not pitching one difficult time against another. We have faced many of them in this place. I actually go back long enough to remember a time of plenty as well in this place, but that was another decade, almost in another century.

On the point you make, though, about needing to properly now assess where we are in terms of fiscal equality and meeting the economic and social needs of Wales through the Barnett formula as it is currently, our view as a Government is that the Barnett formula needs review. My immediate view on that—and it's something that I shared with the previous finance Minister—is that the Barnett formula especially needs its operational aspects to be strengthened. So, we need greater transparency on the Barnett formula as it exists, as well as independent oversight of the Barnett formula, so that we never ever again have to deal with the fiasco as it was of the decision on HS2 and how that has underfunded us as a country. And on that, if not on any other issue, I hope that we can all unite.

So, I'm not pitching one difficult time against another. We have faced many of them in this place. I actually go back long enough to remember a time of plenty as well in this place, but that was another decade, almost in another century.

On the point you make, though, about needing to properly now assess where we are in terms of fiscal equality and meeting the economic and social needs of Wales through the Barnett formula as it is currently, our view as a Government is that the Barnett formula needs review. My immediate view on that—and it's something that I shared with the previous finance Minister—is that the Barnett formula especially needs its operational aspects to be strengthened. So, we need greater transparency on the Barnett formula as it exists, as well as independent oversight of the Barnett formula, so that we never ever again have to deal with the fiasco as it was of the decision on HS2 and how that has underfunded us as a country. And on that, if not on any other issue, I hope that we can all unite.

Diolch. I'd like to declare an interest, as I'm looking forward to becoming a trustee of the Living Room in the near future.

On 11 September this year, the Living Room in Cardiff celebrated 15 years of transforming people's lives. It was established by Wynford Ellis Owen with the support of the Welsh Council on Alcohol and Other Drugs, which itself is now marking 55 years of service. Since the beginning, the centre has offered hope to people living with addiction and harmful behaviours, as well as supporting their families and their local community.

Through counselling, therapeutic groups, peer support and education, thousands of people have had the opportunity to rebuild their lives. Stafell Fyw demonstrates that recovery is possible when people are treated with dignity, compassion and respect. It also highlights the value of investing in our community services, preventing problems from escalating and reducing pressure on our health, social care and criminal justice services.

As we mark this milestone, I'd like to thank the staff, volunteers, trustees and everyone who has contributed to the work of the Living Room over the last 15 years. Above all, I'd like to pay tribute to the individuals in recovery who remind us every day that change is possible and that hope is stronger than addiction.

On Saturday, I was pleased to attend the official launch of the Football Museum of Wales and Wrexham Museum. As a member for Fflint Wrecsam, it was a real pleasure to be part of such an important occasion for the area and to join with colleagues in seeing the Cabinet Minister cut the ribbon on the museum.

The launch was a fantastic opportunity to celebrate the heritage of Wrexham and the history of Welsh football, and to see the new galleries and the stories they have to tell. I'm sure many of us agree that football is such an important part of communities across Wales. It brings people together, sometimes drives them apart, but creates shared opportunities and is a huge part of our national identity. The Football Museum of Wales provides a fantastic opportunity to preserve that history and share it with future generations.

The Wrexham Museum also plays an important role in celebrating the city, its people and its heritage. I was particularly pleased to meet those involved in making these museums a reality and to see the pride and enthusiasm surrounding the launch. These museums have huge potential to attract visitors, support the local economy and showcase Wrexham to people from across Wales and beyond. I hope the Welsh Government will recognise that potential and continue to work with and support both museums as they establish themselves and grow. They are important cultural assets for Wrexham and for Wales and deserve every opportunity to succeed.

I would like to pay tribute to the work of the RSPCA during the summer hot weather and the work that they do to safeguard our pets and animals, especially dogs. Dogs can struggle badly in hot weather because they cool themselves mainly by panting, not sweating like humans. That means that even a warm day can become dangerous, especially for flat-faced breeds such as pugs and bulldogs, older dogs, overweight dogs and those with heart or breathing problems.

Owners should always make sure that dogs have constant access to fresh water, shade and a cool place to rest indoors or outside. Walks should be planned for the early morning or late evening when the ground and air are cooler. Hot pavements and asphalt can burn paws quickly, so it is wise to test the surface before going out. Dogs should never be left in a parked car, conservatory or other enclosed hot space, even for a few minutes, because temperatures can rise to fatal levels very fast. Grooming can also help in summer, but dogs should not usually be shaved without veterinary advice, as their coats can protect them from both sun and overheating.

It is also important to know the signs of heatstroke: heavy panting, drooling, weakness, vomiting, confusion and collapse, which are all warning signs that need urgent veterinary attention. If a dog seems overheated, move it to a cooler area, offer water and contact a vet immediately. The RSPCA in Wales deserves real praise for promoting practical, compassionate advice on dog welfare during hot weather. Its guidance is clear, accessible and focused on prevention, helping owners to understand simple but life-saving steps. By raising awareness about heatstroke, hot cars and safe summer care, the RSPCA continues to play an important role in protecting dogs across Wales.

Sir Billy Boston, who passed away last month at the age of 92, was one of rugby league's greatest ever players, an inspiration from Butetown in Cardiff, and I'm sure the whole Chamber will want to share our condolences with the Boston family.

Born on Angelina Street, just a stone's throw from this building, he first played rugby for Cardiff Internationals Athletic Club, and it's great to see the CIACs still going to this day. Billy dreamed of representing Cardiff and Wales through rugby union, yet despite his talent, he was overlooked by his hometown club and nation. As my predecessor Vaughan Gething said,

'It's hard to believe this was simply down to a scouting system failure and nothing to do with the colour of his skin.'

After being spotted during national service, he joined Wigan rugby league where he became a sporting legend. His remarkable achievements for Wigan, Great Britain and the game itself secured his place amongst rugby league's all-time greats. Last year, he became the first rugby league player to be knighted. Last week, Wigan renamed their central square in his honour.

I was immensely proud to work with members of the Butetown community, sports figures and local businesspeople to secure a lasting tribute to Billy and the other code breakers from Cardiff in the statue that was unveiled in Cardiff Bay. We were particularly delighted that we were able to achieve that during Billy's lifetime and have him there with us as we unveiled the statue to him, Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman, a fitting tribute to all the code breakers achieved and all they overcame. Rest in peace, Sir Billy Boston.

Diolch yn fawr, Lywydd. I'd like to move today's motion submitted in the name of my colleague Llŷr Powell, Reform UK. Members of the Chamber, three years ago today, my daughter was held against her will and raped. I say this with her agreement; I will not give the details. I say it because in debates like this, victims are often talked about as a category, a number and a strategy. She's my child. Let me be clear, this was not a grooming gang, it was one man, and let me give the outcome first, because it matters. He is serving 14 years. She was believed.

But it took far too long, the examinations, the statements, the changes of personnel, the waiting for news and the uncertainty when nothing appeared to happen. She kept going. Nothing should underestimate what that required. A conviction matters enormously, but it does not erase what came before or the need for support. That is the perspective that I bring here today.

Now, hold that beside what inquiries have found out about children subjected to organised sexual exploitation. Children disbelieved, children blamed, adults describing abuse as though it were a choice that the child had made. I am not equating my daughter's experience with theirs. I'm asking Members to consider what happens when a victim faces those barriers without someone beside them insisting that they matter.

We do not need to look outside of Wales for evidence. In February 2022, the independent inquiry into child sexual abuse published its investigation into exploitation by organised networks. Swansea was one of the six areas examined. It found that neither the police nor the council accurately understood how many children were experiencing or were at risk of child sexual exploitation. South Wales Police had told the inquiry that there was no data suggesting exploitation by organised networks. The inquiry found examples that should have been identified. It also describes a perpetrator facing similar previous allegations, a case closed with no recorded explanation, no exploitation flag and no application for a sexual risk order, despite evidence suggesting he was a likely candidate. A Welsh city, a national inquiry four years ago. Members should ask what changed after those findings, who checked and whether children are safer as a result, because publishing a finding is only the beginning of accountability.

My daughter had a family that would have done anything for her. For a long time, she did not ask us; she was ashamed. The shame belonged entirely to the man who harmed her, but knowing that as a parent does not mean that you can make your child feel it as well. Abusers use shame to silence people. Fear and manipulation make asking for help impossible. She had somewhere to turn, even when she could not bring herself to turn there. Ask yourselves what happens to a young person who feels that she has nowhere. 

And this is not only a question about historic abuse. On 3 August this year, five defendants were convicted at Caernarfon Crown Court of more than 40 offences, following a North Wales Police investigation. The case concerned the exploitation and abuse of three girls aged 14 to 16 in Rhyl and the surrounding areas between April 2022 and March 2024. Those young women deserve recognition for their courage. The officers who secured those convictions deserve the credit. But successful prosecutions must also prompt us to ask whether opportunities to protect children earlier were missed. We should establish the answer through evidence without prejudging the findings.

The independent inquiry into grooming gangs covers England and Wales. In the first investigations, they are Oldham, Bradford, Keighley and London. Further areas will be selected. No Welsh area is in that initial group, but that does not mean that Wales has been excluded. But families deserve clarity about how Welsh institutional failures will be examined.

There is another question that Ministers should pursue. In June, the National Crime Agency reported that Operation Beaconport had identified closed cases in eight police areas with potentially viable lines of inquiry. Forces were directed to reopen those cases to determine the next steps. So, what is the position in Wales? How many qualifying cases have our forces referred? Have Welsh cases been returned for further action? Ministers should seek that information and publish what can properly be disclosed whilst protecting survivors and investigations.

We must also be precise about this Chamber's responsibilities. Policing and criminal justice, as we know, are not devolved. However, health, education and social services are. This Senedd legislates and scrutinises spending in those areas. Welsh Ministers set safeguarding policies and must answer for their effectiveness. We cannot direct every criminal investigation. We can demand that services around a child recognise abuse, share concerns and act. We can insist that information is recorded consistently so repeated warnings are recognised. We can scrutinise whether survivors receive support through the process and after the verdict. The responsibilities are substantial and they must be exercised.

Investigators must also follow the evidence where it leads. I've heard the excuses before, when not to look, that the numbers in Wales are far lower than elsewhere and that most abuse here is committed by home-grown perpetrators. Both of these things may be true, but neither of them is an answer. A comparison of numbers is not a safeguarding policy. No child was ever protected by the observation that a different kind of offender is more common. And a victim hears that argument exactly the way that it is meant. She hears that her case was small, that she was a rounding error in somebody else's statistic. I'm not asking this Chamber to inflate the scale of anything, I'm asking for Members to stop using scale as a reason not to look. Baroness Casey's audit identified examples of organisations avoiding questions about ethnicity for fear of appearing racist or increasing community tensions. No offender's background, regardless of colour, should place them above scrutiny. The test is the individual, not the community he came from. The standard must be the same. Follow the evidence and protect the child.

Yesterday, in answering my colleague Claire Archibald, the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health spoke about the importance of women being heard and not ignored. I agree with her and I intend to hold her to that principle, because that principle must apply here too. The victims we're talking about today are often girls who are frightened, manipulated and ashamed, girls who may not have the confidence, the words or the power to insist that somebody listens. A girl of 14 is not yet a woman. She should not have to become one before her voice matters. And being heard cannot simply mean somebody listened. It must mean that concerns are recorded, the warning signs are recognised, that referrals are made, information is shared and, when the evidence demands it, that action follows, because a child should not have to keep telling adults that something is wrong until somebody finally believes her.

That is what being heard must mean in safeguarding, and that is the standard to which I intend to hold this Government. So, I ask Ministers for three things. First, publish the substantive correspondence with the Home Office and the inquiry, with necessary protections for confidential information. Let this Chamber see what has been requested and what remains unresolved. Secondly, bring together evidence from safeguarding boards, police and survivors, and make a formal case for examining Welsh institutional failures. Thirdly, if those failures are not adequately examined by the national inquiry, will Ministers establish a Wales-specific statutory inquiry into devolved services? Welsh families deserve a clear answer.

Members of the Chamber, I cannot give my daughter back those three years, nobody here can, but every Member can bring the same seriousness to another family's child that they would bring to their own. The next child in Fishguard, Haverfordwest, Pembroke or anywhere here in Wales—before accepting assurance, think about the child waiting for someone to act. If this were a child you love, what answers would be good enough? Diolch yn fawr.

Diolch, Lywydd. I welcome the motion that's been tabled today by Reform, and I move the amendment tabled in the name of my colleague Paul Davies. I want to thank Paul Marr for the measured way in which he opened this debate and spoke so powerfully about his daughter's personal experience of sexual abuse.

This is an issue that should cut completely across party political barriers. We shouldn't shy away from discussing it, no matter how difficult it might be or how uncomfortable the subject matter is, because there should be no division amongst any of us in this Chamber when it comes to protecting children from rape and sexual exploitation. There shouldn't be any division when it comes to supporting victims who've been robbed of their innocence, and there should be no division on the need to investigate why authorities fail to protect some of the vulnerable children in our society from horrific abuse by paedophiles, no matter what the ethnicity of the perpetrators might be.

Now, grooming gang activity has been a serious problem in the UK, and that includes here in Wales. As many people will know, I first raised this matter here in this Senedd Chamber back in January of 2025, and I called at that time for the then First Minister to support a UK inquiry into grooming gangs. She didn't support one. So, I then called on her, as the First Minister of the Welsh Government, to establish a Wales-wide inquiry. She didn't support one. In response, I was told by the then First Minister that there was no widespread evidence of grooming gang activity here in Wales, and that I should substantiate the serious claims that I had made about brave Welsh victims who'd spoken about their experiences—young girls who'd already spoken out publicly about what had happened to them and the failure of the authorities to protect them; individuals like Emily Vaughn, recruited by a grooming gang here in Wales, trafficked to other parts of the UK. She'd spoken out about being strangled, threatened with a knife, the perpetrators of those crimes then threatening to conduct an arson attack on her home to harm members of her family. She was raped over a thousand times. She lost count of the number of men who abused her and her body. And it's not just Emily, that brave individual who has spoken powerfully about her experiences. As has been said, there's been evidence of exploitation by grooming gangs of children in Swansea, and there's been the recent series of convictions in Rhyl, my own constituency, a case on my own doorstep. Absolutely appalling abuse. Teenagers, young children in our communities given drugs, enticed and abused by men.

Now, the ongoing Operation Oak, of course, has led to some further arrests in Gwent, where there have been 34 offences that people have been charged with, including multiple counts of rapes. And let me tell you, it was speaking to Emily Vaughn and it was reading the accounts of victims that made me all the more determined to make sure that we do everything we can to ensure that these things are not happening in our communities. Every single one of us in this Chamber has a moral obligation to leave no stone unturned in trying to tackle these heinous crimes.

That is why I fully support the motion before the Chamber today. For many years now, I have tried at every opportunity to support and advocate for victims of sexual exploitation and grooming. It is something we should all take very seriously. Sexual grooming is something that, unfortunately, far too many of us have experienced during our formative years. Be it perpetrated by groups or by individuals, it's an insidious crime that leaves victims with a lifetime of shame, guilt and self-blame. That shame, of course, is not for the victims to carry. That shame should change sides.

Abusers are both clever and controlling. Grooming behaviours can be very hard to spot and perpetrators can be exceptionally skilled at hiding their motives. A high-profile investigation into a case of grooming in my constituency revealed that a victim, a schoolgirl, had Googled, 'Is this grooming?', as she tried to understand what was happening to her. Children should never have to rely on a search engine to protect them from the calculating behaviour of a ruthless abuser. That's why I'm so proud that Plaid Cymru has committed to helping children and young people recognise the signs of grooming through the relationships and sexuality education. This is one of the many reasons why RSE is so important. Every child and young person in school has equal access to a vital education that can help keep them safe. It can help them understand and recognise positive, healthy relationships, and, equally, it can alert them to the behaviour of an abuser.

Plaid Cymru stands with each and every victim and survivor of sexual abuse. If you were groomed by a family member, we stand with you. If you were groomed by a person in a position of trust, we stand with you. And if you were groomed by a group of abusers, we stand with you. Sexual abuse steals childhoods, it shatters futures, it pushes victims to the very edge of what they feel they can endure. But I'll tell you what sexual abuse isn't. It is not a political football, it is not clickbait content and it is not culture-war fodder. These are real children, real survivors and real lives, not pawns in someone else's cynical point-scoring game.

I look forward to supporting the actions that will be taken by this Government under the 10-year national strategy for preventing and responding to child sexual abuse, published earlier this year. I look forward to seeing our manifesto commitments at work, which include strengthening the voice of children within safeguarding arrangements and introducing a duty to report child sexual abuse. I look forward to supporting the work that will be done by this Government to strengthen RSE, which is a vital educational tool to help keep children safe. I look forward to seeing the results of the statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs, and supporting this Government's response to any recommendations relating to Wales. I absolutely want to reinforce my support for the victims and survivors of the vile crimes of grooming gangs, as well as my support for all victims and survivors of grooming and sexual exploitation in Wales and beyond. Diolch.
