The last time I stood in this Chamber to speak the uncomfortable truth about the safety of women and girls, Members walked out. So, a trigger warning before I begin. When I stood for election, I promised to stand unapologetically for the safety of women and girls. I intend to keep that promise, and I make no apology for that.

Before entering politics, I served in policing domestically and internationally and I saw first-hand the human reality of trafficking. Once you've seen what human beings are capable of doing to other human beings, you cannot unsee it. Once you have seen institutions from the inside, you develop a very low tolerance for institutional failure.

When the independent inquiry into grooming gangs was announced, I wrote to Baroness Longfield, because the previous independent inquiry into child sexual abuse examined Swansea as its only Welsh case study. I wanted reassurance that Wales would not once again become a footnote, as my colleague has previously said. I received her response. Well, I am not reassured.

Yes, this is a statutory inquiry, Wales is technically within its scope, and, yes, it can compel evidence and witnesses. Its terms of reference examine institutional failure and possible cover-ups. But there's still no guarantee of a dedicated investigation into Wales. I am told the inquiry will visit Wales, meet victims and survivors and establish an office here; Welsh areas may be considered for investigation later. But, Llywydd, an office in Wales is not an investigation of Wales. Listening to Welsh victims is not the same as investigating who failed them.

That matters because this Welsh Government has made integration and community cohesion central to its nation of sanctuary policy. It tells us that its approach helps people integrate with host communities and strengthens community cohesion. Fine. Then let us test that confidence against the evidence. Where evidence shows that culture, ethnicity and religion influenced offending, the targeting of victims, or an institution's willingness to intervene, we must examine it. The inquiry's own terms of reference expressly require those very questions to be examined. This is not prejudice. This is safeguarding. And after some of the comments made in the last 24 hours, perhaps that distinction needs stating particularly clearly.

We have been told that challenging the nation of sanctuary creates division, that Reform is interested in opposition and headlines, and that minorities must not be scapegoated or dehumanised. On one thing, I agree completely: nobody should be dehumanised. But neither should uncomfortable evidence be sanitised because examining it makes politicians uncomfortable. Asking whether children were sexually exploited is not scapegoating, and is most certainly not clickbait. Asking whether institutions failed them is not division, and examining culture, ethnicity or religion where the evidence warrants it is not dehumanising anyone. If scrutiny itself is now to be characterised as division, then institutional failure has found the safest hiding place here. If demanding answers for sexually exploited children generates headlines, perhaps we should ask why the failures did not generate enough headlines in the first place. Because we know the scenario, we know the cycle: reviews, inquiries, recommendations for lessons learned and then other reviews to learn why the lessons were not learnt. Victims deserve better than the carousel of institutional regret. So, my demand is straightforward: guarantee a dedicated Welsh local area investigation under the existing statutory inquiry with its full statutory powers. If that guarantee cannot be given, then Wales must have a dedicated statutory inquiry of its own. This is not duplication; it is accountability.

This Welsh Government tells us that nation of sanctuary policies strengthen integration and community cohesion. Then demonstrate your confidence in them: open the books, open the records and welcome the scrutiny. Plaid Cymru speak endlessly about Wales exercising the powers of a nation—then accept the responsibilities of one. Do not demand the powers of a nation whilst outsourcing the accountability of one, and do not tell Welsh victims that being somewhere within the scope of an England and Wales inquiry is good enough. It isn't. Wales must be investigated and, if others will not look, we will.

Can I start by expressing my thanks to Paul Marr for sharing his family's deeply personal experiences and for setting the tone for this debate so well? I will try and continue in that vein. Can I also thank the charity Action for Children for an incredibly helpful briefing that they shared in advance of this debate? 

Let me be clear: child sexual exploitation is abhorrent. It destroys childhoods, damages families and leaves victims and survivors carrying the consequences for decades. Let me be clear again: whilst victims and survivors deserve justice, they deserve our support and they deserve the opportunity to have their experience heard. There can be no complacency. If women or children are being abused, we must know about it and we must act to stop it.

Wales is already within the scope of the statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs. The published terms of reference state explicitly that the inquiry will cover England and Wales. So, the question is not whether Wales is included—Wales is included, and that is right. It must be the case that Welsh victims are heard. Where necessary, Welsh institutions must be held to account, and the inquiry's findings must lead to meaningful action. The amendment we're supporting puts victims and survivors first. It recognises that people need not only justice but support. It acknowledges the existing scope of the statutory inquiry that holds Welsh Government to account over their commitment to consider carefully any findings and recommendations relating to Wales, taking forward whatever action is necessary, and this place will hold them to account.

This is a sensitive issue. Whenever we discuss it, our focus must be on the experiences and concerns of victims. I don't think this is the place for political point-scoring, because, as Darren said, I think this is an issue on which there is broad consensus. Baroness Casey herself warned about the reluctance of some local areas to face up to the fact that victims had not been treated properly. We must not repeat that failure. We must confront institutional failings wherever they occurred, regardless of the organisation, location or individuals involved, no matter how uncomfortable that may be, and we should also recognise that Wales has already taken significant action.

The last Welsh Government legislated through the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014. That legislation places safeguarding duties on relevant agencies. Where an agency, including the police, probation services or another local authority, has reasonable cause to suspect that a child or an adult with care and support needs is at risk of abuse, neglect or other harm, there is a legal duty to inform the relevant local authority. But, of course, legislation alone is not enough. Duties must be understood, followed and properly monitored, and, where they have not been followed, there must be accountability. That is why we welcomed Baroness Casey's audit and remain committed to engaging fully with its recommendations.

We also recognise work already undertaken through the independent inquiry into child sexual abuse, chaired by Professor Alexis Jay. Organisations, including the Children's Commissioner for Wales and police and crime commissioners, have rightly emphasised the need to implement its recommendations. That work must continue. And the Welsh Government's 10-year strategy for preventing and responding to child sexual abuse in Wales, published in March this year, builds on that foundation. It covers all forms of child sexual abuse, including sexual exploitation, and sets out action on prevention, protection, effective responses and long-term support for adult victim survivors. 

This issue cuts across devolved and reserved responsibilities. Safeguarding, social services, health and education are central Welsh responsibilities, whilst policing, prosecution, court, probation and prisons are reserved to the UK Government. That is why I support the approach currently being taken, and that approach must also be evidence led. A rise in convictions is important and must be understood, but convictions alone do not tell us the full scale or nature of abuse. We must collect and examine all relevant data, including data on the ethnicity of perpetrators. Abuse is abuse and must always be condemned. That does not mean stigmatising entire communities or allowing evidence to be replaced by assumptions.

Victims and survivors have waited too long for justice. They do not need an incorrect suggestion that Wales has been excluded from the inquiry. They need the inquiry to proceed urgently, transparently and with proper attention to Welsh cases. Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Can I start by thanking all of the Members who have shared their powerful stories so far in this debate, especially Paul? Thank you for your deeply moving contribution. The horrors perpetrated by grooming gangs have been seen first-hand in Clwyd, as mentioned by Darren and Paul already. Three teenage girls in Rhyl and the surrounding area were exploited and abused for nearly two years. The court has heard evidence of drug supply, attempts to obstruct justice, rape, sexual assault, child exploitation and modern-day slavery. Individuals aged between 14 and 16 were subjected to these horrific crimes in cars, residential addresses and at a business.

I must commend North Wales Police for catching these vile people. I'm sure the whole Chamber will join with me in condemning them, namely Sarah, Mustafa, Mohamed, Ziaullah and Jaswinder, for the evil that they have undertaken. Not only did they subject the victims to lifelong trauma by taking advantage of their vulnerabilities and seeking to manipulate and control them for their own gain, but by denying the charges, they forced them to relive their ordeal through a lengthy trial.

As the senior investigating officer at North Wales Police explained, and I quote:

'Rather than accepting responsibility for the appalling harm they caused, they forced these young women to endure the additional trauma of a lengthy trial, requiring them to relive their experiences in a courtroom.

'I hope today’s outcome sends a clear message that those who seek to groom and exploit vulnerable children will be relentlessly pursued.'

That is what is required and that is what is not happening here in Wales. Evidence of that is clear from the case that I've just mentioned. One of the individuals who was convicted of conspiracy to traffic and supply drugs was housed by the council in temporary housing, exposing him to other vulnerable people housed at that location and in nearby locations. The local authority's own risk assessment didn't flag any allegations. It didn't flag the police investigation or the arrest. That is alarming, Members. How many other people under investigation have been placed in inappropriate housing? There appears to have been a significant flaw in information sharing between the police and local authority in this case, likely meaning that the local authority inadvertently placed other people and children at risk.

As I made clear over the summer, the UK statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs in its current form is not the best solution for children and victims in Wales. Whilst the inquiry is undertaking local investigations in Bradford and Keighley, Oldham and London, it doesn't have a single location here in Wales. That fact is incredible when you consider that addressing this evil in our society cannot just be done by the police alone. Instead, it requires a joined-up approach with so many other public services, including housing, local authorities, social services, the health service and our schools, all of which are devolved in Wales. As such, the experience of how these public sector bodies play their part in tackling grooming gangs could be fundamentally different in England than in Wales. Welsh victims and children deserve better. We need Wales's voice to be heard. Welsh victims need to be heard directly.

Members, I urge you to support this motion. It is only through such action that we will pursue grooming gangs relentlessly in Wales.

contributions.text_english:
I too thank Paul Marr for the way he set this debate. That was really important. Because every victim of sexual exploitation, as we've heard, deserves justice. These are some of the most appalling crimes imaginable, and my heart—all of our hearts—goes out to everyone who has been a victim. And that is why this debate is so important.

The recent rise in convictions in Wales should serve as a reminder that this is not an issue that can simply be dismissed or something that happens elsewhere. Recent cases in Wales demonstrate that child sexual exploitation has occurred here in our communities, and that serious questions must continue to be asked about whether agencies always acted as they should have. 

We welcome the UK Government's decision to establish a statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs. It is an important step forward, and one that survivors have campaigned for over many years. But whilst that inquiry is welcome, it cannot be used as an excuse for inaction here in Wales.

Our amendment calls on the Welsh Government to commission a Wales-wide grooming gang inquiry into matters that fall within devolved competence. That is a reasonable request. Indeed, it's difficult to see how anyone could oppose it. contributions.text_english:
There are some words and some subjects that are uncomfortable to discuss. There are words that our politicians and institutions would rather avoid—words like 'grooming gang'—and therein lies the problem. When the safety of children is at stake, discomfort cannot be an excuse for silence. So, in this debate, I want to speak about the organised sexual exploitation of children, which has commonly become known as the 'grooming gang scandal'. 

These words should never be abstract. They are real, and there are real victims of it. Behind every report, every investigation, every statistic, is a child: a child who should have been protected; a child who should have been listened to; far too often, a child who was failed by the very institutions that were designed to keep them safe. 

The independent inquiry into child sex abuse examined organised sexual exploitation across England and Wales. Wales was not absent from its findings, and in the new statutory inquiry, it does not automatically guarantee that a particular Welsh town or local authority will receive a full investigation.

In Swansea, the inquiry was initially told that there was no data suggesting sexual exploitation by networks of gang-related child abuse. In response to our freedom of information request in 2025, Gwent Police acknowledged that they only had the software available since 2017 to search the 6,683 sexual offences recorded, and they were not sure if ethnicity was recorded, and if it was, it would cost too much manpower and time to trawl through the data to search for grooming cases. Yet the inquiry found examples of exploitation by groups that should have been identified by the police. South Wales Police itself acknowledges the likelihood that organised criminal networks existed that had not been discovered. This is shameful. How do we protect our children from something that the authorities fail to identify? We cannot properly understand the threat if we refuse to collect the data to expose it.

The independent inquiry, therefore, made an extremely important recommendation: police forces and local authorities should collect specific information on known and suspected child sexual exploitation networks, including data on sex, ethnicity and disability of victims and perpetrators. And that is not prejudice, it's evidence. If patterns exist, we need to know about them. If particular vulnerabilities are being exploited, we need to know of them. Wherever offenders come from, their ethnicity, religion, background and status, the response should be exactly the same. Protect the child, investigate the crime, prosecute the offender for a long time, and do not let them out early. No excuses, no political sensitivities, no fear of embarrassment, and no institution protecting its reputation ahead of a vulnerable child. We value children above protecting the very systems that let them down.

And we should also remember something fundamental about grooming: children who are manipulated, coerced and exploited are the victims. They are not responsible for the crimes committed against them. A frightened teenager who has been groomed by adults does not need an institution finding reasons not to intervene. They need an adult to listen. They need professionals to recognise the warning signs, and they need the state to act. This means schools, social services, health professionals, local authorities and police sharing information effectively.

Let's narrow this down to Wales. So, where are the Welsh authorities targeted for investigation in the statutory review? So far, there aren't any. Are we to be pushed back again, not listening in Wales again? Are the victims ever going to get the justice that they deserve in Wales? In short, we want data accuracy; we want transparency; Welsh voices to be heard; and they must not be silenced ever again.

I wanted to address those who truly matter at the centre of this: the women and children who have survived group-based sexual exploitation. I want to speak to everyone who has been in a vulnerable position and let down by those in power who were meant to be there to protect them.

My mum was barely 15 when she went to her GP and told him she was pregnant. His only advice was, 'Go home and tell your parents.' She was alone, she was frightened, and she hid it. Her teachers watched and shook their heads as the gossip spread around school while she used a ribbon to extend her school skirt around her growing baby. And three weeks after turning 16, my mum gave birth, and that was the first time that she'd been properly cared for by those who should have protected her. Too often, girls like my mum are judged on their bad choices rather than seen as children who needed help. I want every survivor to know that I hear you, I see you, and I believe you. You deserve support, and you deserve justice.

Quite often, what we've heard in debates is Reform inciting fear in minority groups. What we want to do is focus on what we would do to improve lives in Wales. It's so important that that is our focus. We all wish to make sure that we treat women as equal in our society and equal in this Chamber. We wish to hear and listen to every voice.

Reform position themselves as 'outside of the establishment', which obscures its own role in maintaining the political culture where male violence flourishes. This culture starts with harmless banter and women being spoken over, but it can escalate into intimidation, harassment, abuse and sexual violence. Here in Wales, specialist violence against women, domestic abuse and sexual violence services have warned of rising demand and increasingly complex high-risk cases, reminding us that violence against women is not an abstract issue, but a daily reality for far too many.

The system is still, too often, failing to deliver justice and protection, and changing that should be our collective commitment. Safety is not a slogan, it's a priority. Group-based abusers do not respect borders. We've heard how survivors have been trafficked across the UK and into Wales and out of Wales, so it's vital that we hear from everybody who has been in our country. This ensures that perpetrators are held to account.

Plaid Cymru's amendment is the right course of action because it puts victims and survivors first. Rather than duplicating efforts with a separate inquiry, we can work within the existing statutory framework to focus on what actually makes a difference—delivering the actions of the national strategy for prevention and responding to child sexual abuse. This is how we ensure that women and girls get the justice and support that they deserve.

The victims of these appalling crimes and their families deserve the truth. I'll begin by paying tribute to my colleague Paul Marr for the powerful and courageous way in which he opened this debate. Every Member here present, and those that could not be, should imagine being the victim or the parent fighting for answers, only to be ignored or failed by the authorities that are meant to protect them.

Grooming gangs represent some of the most sickening organised criminality our country has witnessed. Unless we establish the full scale of what has happened and confront the failures that allowed it to happen, we cannot protect children going forward. Last year, the Welsh Government claimed there were no current widespread issues with grooming gangs in Wales. Let's have a look at the past 10 weeks alone.

On 10 July, Azad Ahmed and Wasee Shikel were imprisoned in Cardiff. On 15 July, eight men were charged across south Wales as part of Operation Oak. On 3 August, five people in Rhyl were convicted of grooming gang offences. That is why our motion calls on the UK Government to ensure that Wales is investigated at the earliest opportunity as part of the statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs. Victims in Wales deserve the same truth, the same justice and the same accountability as victims elsewhere in the United Kingdom. Those cases demand answers. How can the Welsh Government confidently claim there is no widespread problem when serious gaps remain in the evidence?

Reports elsewhere in Britain have identified cases involving predominantly Pakistani-heritage Muslim men targeting white British girls. For years, legitimate questions about those patterns were avoided by the authorities, who seemed more concerned about causing offence than protecting children. We cannot allow political correctness or institutional cowardice to stand in the way of safeguarding.

If similar patterns exist in Wales, they must be exposed. Transparent data on offender ethnicity is essential to understanding the threat and preventing further abuse. The Welsh Government must also scrutinise every relevant policy, including its nation of sanctuary approach, to ensure proper safeguards prevent dangerous individuals from entering or remaining in our communities.

An abuser is an abuser. Correct. Yes. 

Compassion cannot mean naivety. Anyone who comes to this country must respect our laws, our culture, and the rights of women and girls. We need to know whether social services, police forces and local authorities failed in their duty of care, whether warning signs were ignored, and most importantly, what has changed. Victims have waited far too long. They deserve truth, justice and accountability, and this Senedd must not rest until they receive them.

That's the speech over, but I've got a few minutes, so I've got free reign, Llywydd, if you don't mind. Some of the voices here today have been brilliant, and they've got to the heart of the problem. We have an issue going on across our land, and we need to grasp that mantle and do whatever we need to do to ensure our future generations and our young children now are safe and kept safe. There have been some brilliant points made from across the parties. Beca, I agree with many of the points that you made. This should not be a political football; it's a shame you never got the memo.

contributions.text_english: This debate deals with some of the most serious harms, the most horrific harms a child can experience. Child sexual abuse and child sexual exploitation can have a profound and lifelong impact on every aspect of a person's life. These issues can affect education, relationships, employment, physical health, mental health and well-being of an individual well into adulthood. Those who commit these crimes must be held to account. All victims and survivors deserve justice and help.

contributions.text_english:
Before I go further, Llywydd, I want to acknowledge the courage of victims and survivors whose experiences continue to shape our understanding of abuse and exploitation and drive improvements across our safeguarding systems. I am in awe of your bravery, and I am committed to ensuring that your voices are heard and that your experiences continue to drive change.

The motion before us notes the recent rise in convictions relating to sexual exploitation by grooming gangs in Wales and states that all Welsh victims deserve justice. On that principle, there should be no disagreement in this Chamber. I would counter that it is not enough. Justice usually means a moment in time where people who have done awful things are held to account. That is vitally important. But in and of itself, it is not a deliverance. Survivors need the right support at the right time throughout their life and more than just that moment. That is why our amendment has added that crucial component of support.

The Government amendment further recognises that Wales falls within the scope of the statutory independent inquiry into grooming gangs, which has been established on an England and Wales basis. This Government is committed to considering carefully any findings and recommendations relating to Wales, and to progressing any necessary action with the utmost urgency. The amendment also reaffirms this Government's commitment to addressing child sexual abuse through the national strategy for preventing and responding to child sexual abuse in Wales 2026-2036, published in March this year, including implementing actions set out in its delivery plan.

Vital work has been undertaken in this area, building on the foundations that were laid previously, and the Government is engaging proactively with the inquiry. I hear the concerns raised around the Chamber—I hear them. We are undertaking and continuing official engagement, but I also have a forthcoming meeting with Baroness Longfield, and I will be raising these points. The inquiry has begun announcing areas for local investigation, as we've heard, and we do expect further areas to be announced as its work progresses. Wales already falls within the scope of the statutory inquiry, which can undertake detailed local investigations where the evidence warrants it. Indeed, as I say, I will be reinforcing the need for Wales to be considered fully when I meet the Baroness.

In terms of the motion, there are things we needed to add, like that point I was making about the support as well as justice, and recognising what this Government is doing.

Participation in a wider England and Wales inquiry also provides an opportunity to identify the trends and patterns of abuse that do not respect national borders.

Learning lessons from this inquiry will be essential, but it's also very important that we respond to today's reality. The children who are at risk today can't wait for the conclusions of the inquiry. Alongside our work for the inquiry, we are doing a lot of work to strengthen safeguarding arrangements across Wales, and Members will hear more about that in the coming weeks. I look forward very much to bringing that forward.  

The Welsh Conservatives have tabled an amendment calling for an all-Wales and separate inquiry for devolved issues. I understand the intention that is behind that proposal—I do understand that. It's important to clarify, as I've said, that the inquiry is for England and Wales, but Wales is a central part of its remit. The inquiry has the ability to conduct local investigations in Wales, and it recognises the responsibilities that are devolved and that are not devolved. You were talking about the COVID inquiry, and I think that's the big difference, because that related to the health service predominantly, and that comes under the Welsh Government's remit. That is the difference—[Interruption.] Darren wants to come in.

Ochr yn ochr â’n gwaith ar gyfer yr ymchwiliad, dŷn ni’n gwneud llawer o waith i gryfhau trefniadau diogelu ar draws Cymru, a bydd Aelodau yn clywed rhagor am hynny yn ystod yr wythnosau nesaf. Mae’r Ceidwadwyr Cymreig wedi cyflwyno gwelliant yn galw am ymchwiliad Cymru gyfan ac ar wahân i faterion wedi’u datganoli. Dwi’n deall y bwriad tu ôl i’r cynnig—dwi yn deall hynny. Mae’n bwysig ei gwneud yn glir, fel dwi wedi dweud, bod yr ymchwiliad ar gyfer Lloegr a Chymru. Mae Cymru’n rhan ganolog o’i gylch gwaith. Mae gan yr ymchwiliad y gallu i gynnal ymchwiliadau lleol yng Nghymru, ac mae’n cydnabod y cyfrifoldebau sydd wedi’u datganoli ac sydd ddim wedi'u datganoli. I'm very grateful to you for taking the intervention. There's a direct parallel here, isn't there? Your party stood alongside my party calling for a Wales-specific COVID inquiry, because even though the UK COVID inquiry was charged with investigating matters in Wales, we did not believe that it was going to pay sufficient regard to the decision-making processes in Wales and those devolved areas of competence. Exactly the same applies here.

You've already said that you've had communications with Baroness Longfield about the local inquiries. Well, I will repeat, because this bears repetition, if I have already got to this point: child sexual exploitation does not stop at national borders. Understanding the full picture requires evidence to be examined across the range of agencies involved in safeguarding, education, health, policing and criminal justice too. Not all of those are, of course, devolved to us in Wales. What will, what must make children safer is acting on evidence, identifying risks earlier, strengthening safeguarding practice and ensuring that survivors receive the trauma-informed support that they need.

Now, the 'Strategy for Preventing and Responding to Child Sexual Abuse in Wales 2026-2036' explicitly includes action to prevent, identify and respond to group-based sexual exploitation, including grooming gangs. Together with its delivery plan, it sets out a clear ambition that all children in Wales should live free from the harm of child sexual abuse, and that everyone affected by abuse is protected and supported throughout their lives. That is the ambition. We must deliver it, because, collectively, we need to do more and do it better. That is on all of us.

contributions.text_english:
We will need a whole-system approach, bringing public services, safeguarding partners, communities and survivors together. We will implement a national training framework, strengthen support for practitioners and survivors, and improve services across Wales.

In September alone, more than 400 professionals from all over Wales came together with partners and safeguarding experts to strengthen knowledge, improve practice and promote the implementation of the strategy. At the beginning of next year, an annual national awareness campaign will be launched to help people recognise the signs of abuse and to understand the steps that they can take.

Because safeguarding is everyone's business. Although policing and criminal justice remain reserved issues, we work closely with partners across public services to prevent harm, reduce crime and build safer communities across Wales. This work is also in line with our wider commitment to preventing violence, abuse and exploitation and to creating safer communities across Wales.

We will publish a new strategy on violence against women, domestic abuse and sexual violence during the summer of 2027.

Earlier this year, I shared my priorities with the Senedd. Strengthening safeguarding arrangements to protect children and adults who are at risk is still one of my main priorities. Children's voices must be central to safeguarding decisions, including where concerns exist but the child has not formally disclosed that.

We are committed to introducing new duties in terms of reporting child sexual abuse, strengthening safeguarding standards and ensuring that lessons from safeguarding concerns lead to improvements throughout Wales. During the next few weeks, Members will be able to hear more about how we intend to fulfil those commitments on the floor of the Senedd.

Mi fydd angen dull gweithredu system gyfan, gan ddod â gwasanaethau cyhoeddus, partneriaid diogelu, cymunedau a goroeswyr at ei gilydd. Mi fyddwn ni’n rhoi fframwaith hyfforddi cenedlaethol ar waith, yn cryfhau cymorth i ymarferwyr a goroeswyr, ac yn gwella gwasanaethau ledled Cymru.

Ym mis Medi yn unig, daeth mwy na 400 o weithwyr proffesiynol o bob cwr o Gymru a phartneriaid ac arbenigwyr diogelu at ei gilydd i gryfhau gwybodaeth, gwella ymarfer a hybu’r gwaith o weithredu’r strategaeth. Ar ddechrau’r flwyddyn nesaf, mi fydd ymgyrch codi ymwybyddiaeth genedlaethol flynyddol yn cael ei lansio i helpu pobl i adnabod arwyddion o gam-drin a deall y camau y gallan nhw eu cymryd.

Oherwydd mae diogelu yn fusnes i bawb. Er bod plismona a chyfiawnder troseddol yn parhau i fod yn faterion a gedwir yn ôl, rŷn ni’n gweithio’n agos gyda phartneriaid ar draws gwasanaethau cyhoeddus i atal niwed, lleihau troseddu ac adeiladu cymunedau mwy diogel ledled Cymru. Mae’r gwaith hwn hefyd yn cyd-fynd â’n hymrwymiad ehangach i atal trais, cam-drin a chamfanteisio ac i greu cymunedau mwy diogel ledled Cymru.

Mi fyddwn ni’n cyhoeddi strategaeth newydd ar drais yn erbyn menywod, cam-drin domestig a thrais rhywiol yn ystod yr haf flwyddyn nesaf.

Yn gynharach eleni, fe wnes i rannu fy mlaenoriaethau â’r Senedd. Mae cryfhau trefniadau diogelu i amddiffyn plant ac oedolion sy’n wynebu risg yn dal i fod yn un o’m prif flaenoriaethau. Rhaid i leisiau plant fod yn ganolog i benderfyniadau diogelu, gan gynnwys pan fo pryderon yn bodoli ond dyw'r plentyn ddim wedi datgelu hynny’n ffurfiol.

Rydyn ni wedi ymrwymo i gyflwyno dyletswyddau newydd o ran rhoi gwybod am gam-drin plant yn rhywiol, cryfhau safonau diogelu a sicrhau bod gwersi o bryderon diogelu yn arwain at welliant ledled Cymru. Yn ystod yr wythnosau nesaf, bydd yr Aelodau yn cael clywed rhagor am sut rŷn ni’n bwriadu cyflawni’r ymrwymiadau hynny ar lawr y Senedd.

Llywydd, safeguarding is fundamental to the Wales we want to be. It will continue to be central to this Government's wider ambitions. The Government amendment recognises the seriousness, the terrible seriousness, of these crimes. It recognises that victims and survivors deserve justice and support. It recognises that Wales is within the scope of the statutory inquiry and it commits us—it commits us—to considering carefully any findings and recommendations relating to Wales, and progressing any necessary action.

But importantly, it also focuses on the actions needed to make children safer today. Recent cases we've seen in Wales demonstrate that the responsibility to improve safeguarding, to improve children's lives, begins now. That is why we're strengthening safeguarding arrangements across Wales. That is why safeguarding remains one of my central priorities as Deputy Minister. Because every child deserves to grow up safely. Every victim and survivor deserves to be heard, to be supported, to be treated with dignity. That is the Wales we want, a Wales where children are safer, where abuse is identified earlier, a Wales where survivors receive the support they need throughout their lives, a Wales where survivors receive what they need, where safeguarding arrangements are strong, are effective, are trusted. It is the Wales we must build together, and for those reasons, Llywydd, I ask Members to support the Government amendment.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Can I start by thanking all Members who tried to contribute to the spirit of how we hoped today's debate would go? Paul, your bravery inspires us all. What you and your family went through, what you still go through, and to have the courage to walk in this Chamber today and share those experiences, to try to convince Members of the importance of voting for this motion, is a true inspiration to us all. Thank you so much.

Beca Brown, your contribution: I agreed with most of it until the political point-scoring decided to come out, but education is completely right. I agree with you. And there we can find common ground, but that's not enough. There are victims now who've already had these experiences, and what they want is to be heard, to be listened to, and their voices then can turn into action when people like us in this Chamber hear those experiences. There are people today in the gallery and watching this debate at home who are very keen on expressing their experiences in a safe environment, where it's not politicised, where they're listened to, and where action can be delivered. We can't undermine that.

Now, Darren, your motion today—on these benches, we do agree with you that Wales does need its own COVID inquiry, for the points made by several Members today. The reason we didn't include it in this motion is that we thought we could find consensus across the Chamber that there is currently an inquiry, which is called the England and Wales inquiry, which doesn't currently look at anywhere in this nation.

Now, Minister, I understand you said you're going to make the case for it, but I don't understand your amendment today. Can you imagine the power that we could have sent? You could have had a mandate from this very Chamber, uniting us. You would not have been walking in there as a Minister of a minority Government, you'd have walked through that door with a mandate from this Senedd that says, 'Wales should be included.' There should not be a policy here that we're going to learn from what's happening over in England. Is this now the policy of Plaid Cymru?

On Monday, you were sitting with separatists. Today, you're sitting here saying, 'For Wales, see England.' It's not right. Voices must be heard. And those victims have their own experiences—unique. And I'm sure across Wales they're just as unique in different areas. We couldn't pinpoint one area of Wales that has one experience. The contributions from Darren and Tom today, talking about their constituency—experiences there are horrific. But I'm sure it's unique to that area that has a right to be heard, just like Newport—different again. Let's encourage now together. Let's end this amendment. Let's vote together and give you a clear mandate. That's what these victims want, not point scoring. This isn't clickbait. My colleagues on these benches, like Cristiana, wrote herself to the Chair of the committee urging for this to happen; as Darren said, he's done too. We've written to the Home Secretary urging for Wales to be in there. We're looking to give you today the power to walk into that office with a mandate from this Chamber, this Senedd, the elected Members saying, 'Wales must be included.' So, I urge you to think again. Take this opportunity. Take this cross-party consensus. Let's stand up for the victims. Let's not be tribal in this. That's my offer to you today in voting with us for this motion.

It's so shocking that—. I've had letters back from the chair of this inquiry. How on earth can £65 million be allocated under the name of England and Wales and not one county at the moment looked at? Just the offer of 'maybe'—'maybe it could be'. That's unacceptable. Victims and survivors from other inquiries have said how important having their voices in those inquiries were, whether it's COVID, Hillsborough—the list goes on. Inquiries are an important part of recovery, and that's what we must start thinking about. Recovery—I'm glad Members have mentioned it today, and, Minister, I do agree with you—from mental health and physical trauma, and to those victims who have turned to, whether it's substance abuse, we must do better there to support them. And Sarah Rees, your contribution there, it was a really powerful one at the start. I'm sorry it went a little bit tribal then, but I'm glad you raised those issues, and thank you.

There is more that we must do—we know that in this Chamber. And there is a consensus here. So, when we go forward, looking to what's happening here, let's look at the victims, as Paul said, not as statistics, as human beings—someone's daughter or, in some cases, son, someone's child. That is the power of what we have in front of us today. Now, I know it's not legally binding, this motion in the Chamber, but it's a signal we can send, as a united Senedd, saying that victims across Wales will be and must be listened to, that there isn't anyone who can ignore them any longer, and any predator out there will know that this Senedd won't stand for it. Wales won't stand for it.

contributions.text_english:
The £65 million is allocated by the UK Government. It's a strange scenario; the finance Minister here should be quite happy that Reform isn't asking her to spend any money from the Welsh budget today. We must be included in there, and I hope, when you do meet the chair of the inquiry and other members, that the case is made clearly. And we need to do it without anything else but seeking truth. I don't want anything else—slurs or racism or anything else. All I want in this—and where I agree with the Chair of the committee—is to follow the evidence. Let's empower the police to do what they must do. But we will be voting with the Conservatives on their amendment today, because I believe that there are other cases that we need to get to the bottom of in Wales, whichever layer of body that is.

Cristiana raised several points there that I think should be listened to, and she's raised this passionately time and time again. I hope, when we do leave this Chamber today, we can say that victims will not be ignored. I've heard it across the Chamber, but that isn't enough, us standing here saying it—me standing here saying it isn't. How we vote tonight is what matters. Action from this is what matters.

I heard a powerful story before this debate was tabled, by someone I'm going to call Jane. She's a survivor herself. She was ignored when she talked about her experiences. She was used as what she described as a sexual object, not a human being. From her experience, from what they were doing when they were drugging her—that addiction continued after. The way society labelled her, and what she was—as a drug addict, and a slur, Llywydd, that I will not say in the Chamber, but Members can imagine. Today she has found her way to speak out, to work for a charity helping other people. Her experience has helped more and more young women, women who have come to terms with being able to speak out, to come to terms with what happened and begin their recovery process. And she's watching now and I would like it on the record, which is why I'm saying it, her bravery and actions, and how she's turned a horrific, horrific crime that was made against her, into a positive and a better way of society should inspire us all. For me, it encouraged me to speak out today in this Chamber. And that's the power of speaking out. That's the power of one person speaking to me, to inspire me to speak out in this Chamber today. By letting those victims or survivors—however they wish to be referred to—into that inquiry to be heard is vital. It could inspire another generation, it could open up a lot of eyes into ways we've never considered, or maybe we've walked past blindly.

So, I urge Members, in closing today, to consider what the motion in front of them is. We're not trying to point score. We're not trying to politicise something. We have taken real experiences, listened to real voices and we're urging you today to send a clear signal to the chair of the inquiry: let Wales in. And if you vote to silence us today on that, we will be back, because these voices must be heard. Diolch yn fawr, Lywydd.

contributions.text_english: We will now move to item 6, the Reform UK debate on the Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board health visitor pay dispute. I now call on Benjamin Hodge Mckenna to move the motion. Benjamin.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen nawr at eitem 6, dadl Reform UK, anghydfod cyflogau ymwelwyr iechyd Bwrdd Iechyd Prifysgol Cwm Taf Morgannwg. Galwaf yn awr ar Benjamin Hodge Mckenna i wneud y cynnig. Benjamin.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I stand today in favour of the Reform motion. Between March and May of last year, Cwm Taf Morgannwg carried out 6,410 health visitor visits. In the same three months this year, there were just 909. That isn't a minor adjustment, it's a complete collapse. Babies are missing their checks, safeguarding referrals are a fraction of last year's levels and charities supporting new mothers say that demand has at least doubled for these services, if not trebled. Children in some of the poorest communities in Wales are paying for a dispute that should have been resolved months ago.

And Plaid Cymru know this. I have in my hand today, Llywydd, a letter signed by the current First Minister. He signed it during the election campaign in April. In this letter, he said that the failure to reach a fair settlement was unacceptable, and he called for immediate action for band 6 health visitors to be upgraded to band 7. In March, the current Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport said that all health visitors should be band 7, not band 6, and that an all-female workforce were being denied the pay that they deserved.

Now, those were warm words from Plaid Cymru in opposition, but that was before they had the power to resolve this issue. Now they do. So what has the party done to solve the problem? The health Minister told this Chamber that the industrial action is a dispute between the health board and Unite that relates to decisions over several years. The Welsh Government has said that this is a regrettable situation that should not have occurred in the first place—quite the change in tone from the immediate action that they urged prior to the election.

Health visitors who voted for Plaid Cymru are now asking if the pre-election assurances they were given were misguided or simply false. I have in my hand, Llywydd, another letter, this one written by Unite the Union. In it, they say:

'Many of us voted and campaigned for Plaid, and placed trust in promises you made that a new approach would be taken to resolve this dispute.

'At best were you reckless with your promises or is the question "Has Plaid Lied?"'

Now, that's not my question. Those are the words of health visitors who are being let down by this Plaid Cymru Government.

Asking both sides to come back to the table is not action; it is an abdication. The Welsh Government needs to take immediate action to resolve this dispute, including a fair pay offer to bring an end to strike action. contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Lywydd. I stand today in favour of the Reform motion. Between March and May of last year, Cwm Taf Morgannwg carried out 6,410 health visitor visits. In the same three months this year, there were just 909. That isn't a minor adjustment, it's a complete collapse. Babies are missing their checks, safeguarding referrals are a fraction of last year's levels and charities supporting new mothers say that demand has at least doubled for these services, if not trebled. Children in some of the poorest communities in Wales are paying for a dispute that should have been resolved months ago.

And Plaid Cymru know this. I have in my hand today, Llywydd, a letter signed by the current First Minister. He signed it during the election campaign in April. In this letter, he said that the failure to reach a fair settlement was unacceptable, and he called for immediate action for band 6 health visitors to be upgraded to band 7. In March, the current Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport said that all health visitors should be band 7, not band 6, and that an all-female workforce were being denied the pay that they deserved.

Now, those were warm words from Plaid Cymru in opposition, but that was before they had the power to resolve this issue. Now they do. So what has the party done to solve the problem? The health Minister told this Chamber that the industrial action is a dispute between the health board and Unite that relates to decisions over several years. The Welsh Government has said that this is a regrettable situation that should not have occurred in the first place—quite the change in tone from the immediate action that they urged prior to the election.

Health visitors who voted for Plaid Cymru are now asking if the pre-election assurances they were given were misguided or simply false. I have in my hand, Llywydd, another letter, this one written by Unite the Union. In it, they say:

'Many of us voted and campaigned for Plaid, and placed trust in promises you made that a new approach would be taken to resolve this dispute.

'At best were you reckless with your promises or is the question "Has Plaid Lied?"'

Now, that's not my question. Those are the words of health visitors who are being let down by this Plaid Cymru Government.

Asking both sides to come back to the table is not action; it is an abdication. The Welsh Government needs to take immediate action to resolve this dispute, including a fair pay offer to bring an end to strike action. Rhun ap Iorwerth said in April that the failure to settle this dispute was unacceptable. Those words were true then and they are true now. The difference is that now Plaid Cymru have the power to solve this dispute. So, I urge them to use that power and do so. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_original: Galwaf yn awr ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal i gynnig yn ffurfiol gwelliannau 1 a 2, a gyflwynwyd yn enw Heledd Fychan.

contributions.text_english: Formally.
contributions.text_original: Yn ffurfiol.

contributions.text_english: Thank you. I now call on Andrew R.T. Davies to move amendment 3, tabled in the name of Paul Davies.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr. Galwaf ar Andrew R.T. Davies i gynnig gwelliant 3, a gyflwynwyd yn enw Paul Davies.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Presiding Officer. I move the amendment in the name of Paul Davies on the order paper today. I can see the Minister sitting on the Government bench. When this subject first came to this Chamber, you were on the opposition bench on this side of the Chamber, and colleagues of yours who represented the Cwm Taf area ranted at the then Labour health Minister for inaction and not doing anything to call this dispute to an end and put pressure on the health board.

Five months later, you're on the Government bench and you're not doing the work that your leader signed up to during the election campaign. We were out on the steps yesterday, and the health workers and their families were there, five months after this dispute started—not five weeks, when we were, back in March, in this Chamber, discussing this dispute. And the letter was signed in the election period, on 17 April. That's the letter, and your leader's signature is on the bottom in his capacity as leader. So, he signed for all your Members in this Chamber. And yet what do we have? We have health workers in the Cwm Taf health board still on strike, a health board not engaging and a Plaid Cymru Minister who fought a campaign that his leader signed up to bring it to an end. It does remind me of tuition fees and the Lib Dems, to be honest with you, in 2010. If you don't believe in something, you shouldn't sign up to it, Minister. 

The argument here from the health workers is quite simple. They want to be recognised for their professional qualifications. This isn't saying, 'We want 10 per cent', this isn't saying, 'We want 5 per cent', this isn't saying, 'We want 3 per cent', this is the health workers saying that they want their professional qualifications recognised in the 'Agenda for Change' scheme at band 7 instead of band 6. It was done in Scotland in 2019, it can be done in Wales for this vital piece of the jigsaw that is the health family here in Wales. I call on you, Minister, to live up to the pledge that you made at the election, I call on you to live up to the pledges that your Members made in this Chamber back in March, and bring this dispute to an end. Recognise the dedication and commitment that those health workers and health visitors bring to the community of health workers that are so vital to our NHS, and instead of enjoying the power, exercise the responsibility, and use the responsibility that you have with the power that you have to get the health board round the table and get our key workers back to work so that families can be protected in the Cwm Taf health board area, and ultimately the professional qualifications that these dedicated workers have are recognised under the 'Agenda for Change' scheme and they get the band 7 banding that they deserve. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: I call on Vikki Howells to move amendment 4, tabled in the name of Lynne Neagle.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf ar Vikki Howells i gynnig gwelliant 4, a gyflwynwyd yn enw Lynne Neagle.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I formally move amendment 4. 

We proposed our amendment as the original motion misses an important point, and that is the fundamental role that health visitors play in giving children the best start in life. So, I hope that Members across this Chamber will join us in supporting that amendment to recognise the role of those health visitors today. And for us, that cuts to the core of this matter and why it's so important that it's resolved. And it also echoes the views of those health visitors. They are desperate to get back to their important role, providing that universal safeguarding service, and that's in terms of infant development, perinatal mental health and picking up on those early warning signs when things go wrong.

Health visitors are often the first to identify additional learning needs and to have those crucial conversations about immunisation. Without health visitors, postnatal classes are not running in Cwm Taf Morgannwg and mental health support for parents is just not there. Indeed, since the dispute started, there should have been 23,000 routine appointments under the Healthy Child Wales programme across CTM, but only 900 have been provided. When health visitors are on strike, children and families are not getting the support they need. This must change.

Cabinet Minister, I know my colleague Sarah Murphy recently wrote to you about this, and in your reply you say that the Welsh Government does not have the powers to intervene and you cannot become involved in the dispute itself. That's not correct. Welsh Labour and Unite the Union believe Welsh Government needs to instruct CTM to pay health visitors at band 7, as determined by the independent pay evaluation process. [Interruption.] I haven't got long so I won't be able to, I'm sorry. Saying you urge parties to get back around the negotiating table is insufficient. There's nothing to negotiate on here. Band 7 pay has been determined by an independent pay evaluation process. And there are precedents too, as to how you could intervene. Vaughan Gething stepped in in Betsi Cadwaladr to resolve a shift pattern issue for nurses there; Eluned Morgan sacked non-executive members of the same health board when she wasn't happy with their work. So, we urge you to look at these precedents, listen to Unite and the health visitors they represent, use the powers you have under section 12 of the NHS Act, and not listen to those siren voices urging caution. Your immediate predecessor, Jeremy Miles, made a very clear instruction to CTM that they need to honour that job evaluation process. And as they've not done so, Cabinet Minister, you must step up. By saying you can't intervene, that it's not an issue for Government, you set a dangerous precedent for all NHS staff who come under 'Agenda for Change', from nurses to radiographers to porters to cleaners.

I've had so many e-mails from constituents about this issue. Many voted for your party, some perhaps swayed by the intervention of your party leader on this issue, not least in this letter referred to in the Conservative amendment. In that, your leader wrote, during the election campaign, that the current situation cannot be allowed to continue. He called for immediate action to bring this dispute to a close. Well, you are in power now, Cabinet Minister. The buck stops with you. We've all seen the open letter from Unite the Union deploring your Government's inaction. We in Welsh Labour have stood on the Senedd steps, alongside striking health visitors, each and every time they've demonstrated here, and we've seen their T-shirts bearing the slogan 'Plaid lied’, and heard that chant echo around our Parliament. The First Minister said the ongoing failure to reach a fair settlement is unacceptable—

contributions.text_english:
For many families, health visitors are a vital source of support during some of the most important and sometimes most difficult periods of their lives. This is highly skilled, highly responsible clinical work, and I am concerned that there are significant safeguarding risks posed by the fact that child and family health are not being prioritised by Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board in some of the most deprived and vulnerable parts of Wales. The way in which the health visitors have been treated by the health board is utterly contemptible, and their recent social media post regarding the dispute is an example of the inflammatory and derogatory language they've used to describe the dispute.

Having met and spoken to the health visitors repeatedly throughout this dispute, I know that industrial action is not taken lightly. Strike action is a last resort—it always is. But, ultimately, responsibility for resolving this dispute lies with the health board. This is a dispute of its own making, and it is for the health board to engage meaningfully with its workforce and find a resolution, and that needs to happen now.

The Cabinet Minister for Health and Care has repeatedly urged the health board and Unite to come together to resolve this dispute and minimise the impact on babies, families and staff. There remains a clear commitment to encouraging positive partnership working at every level, and to seeing this dispute resolved through negotiation as soon as possible.

And I find it extraordinary that Reform has suddenly tried to position itself as the party of workers' rights. Where have they been until now? If Reform genuinely believe this issue is so important, they could have been listening to the workers themselves and hearing directly about their concerns from the start of this dispute. And I know for a fact that hasn't been the case. Little wonder, maybe, from a party whose boss wants to axe the Employment Rights Act 2025 and has little regard for equality, diversity and inclusion policies.

But I'll finish, Llywydd, by saying this: we stand firmly with our health visitors and we will continue to support them in this dispute. The message from us is clear: the health board must take responsibility for the situation it has created, engage meaningfully with its workforce and resolve this dispute.

contributions.text_english:
In Rhondda and Ogmore, a health visitor is often the first to notice a baby not feeding, a mother not coping, a home not safe. I accept that the board is the employer and banding must follow NHS job evaluation—the Cabinet Minister cannot sign a payslip. But this dispute has outlasted three First Ministers, and the fourth signed the demand himself—a joint open letter, on 17 April, calling for band 7. Health visitors have now publicly called on him to honour that support. Unite said the board's grading matched the roles to band 7. The board says its revaluation contains band 6. Publish the date, job descriptions, evaluation, records, scores and review rights; explain the differences. That is where a fair offer starts.

Amendment 4 replaces a call for immediate action with recognition of negotiations and the Chief Nursing Officer for Wales's review. In August, the health unions refused to take part in that job description work. Their reason: social partnership has broken down.

My freedom of information request asked whether maternity staff were deployed into health visiting between 23 February and 4 August, when Tirion's suspension was announced. The board's 8 September response did not address that question. My 9 September follow-up requested an answer by 23 September.

Cabinet Minister, on 17 June, you told this Chamber you'd expect the parties to get back around the table. Three months later, what has your personal intervention achieved? What still prevents agreement? When will that review report? And what has this Government done in four months to act on the First Minister's own signature?

I ask for three commitments. First, within 14 days, publish the banding records and a resolution timetable naming who is accountable. Secondly, publish verified monthly figures for contacts due, completed and outstanding, alongside safeguarding referrals by council area and a recovery plan prioritising children at greatest risk. Thirdly, demonstrate that cover arrangements are safe, supervised and do not weaken other services. Families need to know when help will reach them. Staff need to know when their case will be decided. This Government needs to answer both. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I have written and rewritten this contribution because I want to support health visitors as strongly and constructively as I can. I also want to make a declaration that I did work nationally for the NHS before coming into this post. Some are my constituents and all provide care, support and reassurance to families across the communities served by Cymru Taf Morgannwg University Health Board. At its heart, this dispute is about people: the health visitors who feel undervalued and unheard; the children and families who rely on their support; and the communities that depend on a strong, trusted and sustainable health visiting service.

The past few months have been deeply difficult. I know that decisions health visitors have faced have not been taken lightly. Some have contacted me directly, and I have spoken to others on the steps of the Senedd and followed what has been shared publicly. I have heard their frustration, I see the anger, and I recognise the pressure and the hurt this dispute has caused.

Nor is it lost on me that once again we find ourselves debating the value of highly skilled work carried out predominantly by women. Health visitors support new parents through some of the most challenging periods of their lives. They safeguard vulnerable children, identify concerns before they become crises, and provide vital reassurance when families need it most. That work deserves recognition and full respect.

As a first-time mother to twins during the pandemic, our health visitor was one of the very few people who met my children during the first half of the year they were born. At a time that was isolating and uncertain, she was an immense source of support, reassurance and practical guidance when we couldn't see many of our own family members. That experience showed me just how important health visiting services are. For many families, particularly those experiencing poverty, isolation and vulnerability, that early intervention and support can make a lifelong difference.

They are highly skilled professionals and that carries significant responsibility. They make difficult judgments every day and play a vital role in building strong and resilient communities, yet many see the value of that expertise not being fully recognised. I understand why this causes frustration. But these concerns are rooted in local circumstances and local decisions. A lasting resolution will come through meaningful negotiation, not an externally imposed settlement. Unite must continue to engage constructively and in good faith, but the primary responsibility for rebuilding trust and resolving this dispute rests with the health board.

Looking beyond the immediate dispute, we must remain open-minded about the future of health visiting services, including the case for progression to band 7 and band 8 nationally. But any such decision must be grounded in robust clinical evidence, and that is why I welcome the work commissioned by the chief nursing officer as an important first step. While this work continues, the priority must be a fair and durable resolution; one that recognises the value of health Ministers—sorry, 'health visitors'; it's been a long day—and that restores confidence for families. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: I now call on the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, Mabon ap Gwynfor.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf nawr ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal, Mabon ap Gwynfor.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. I welcome the opportunity to respond to this debate. I'll start by endorsing what has already been said about the vital role that health visitors have in supporting babies, children and families across Wales. Their work is often done with some of the most vulnerable families in our communities, and they make an invaluable contribution to improving outcomes and reducing inequality.

I also want to acknowledge the impact that this ongoing dispute has had on the health visitors themselves, on families who rely on their services and on colleagues working across the wider health and care system. I know that the decision to strike would not have been an easy decision for them. The Government understands the strength of feelings on this issue and the concern that has been expressed by Members across the Chamber.

However, it is important that this debate is based on facts. This dispute did not arise overnight. It predates the current Government and it's an issue that has been going on for several years. At the heart of the dispute is a disagreement between Unite and Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board regarding the evaluation of the roles of health visitors and the appropriate pay band arrangements.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Lywydd. Dwi'n croesawu'r cyfle i ymateb i'r ddadl yma. Mi wnaf i ddechrau drwy ategu'r hyn sydd eisoes wedi cael ei ddweud am y rôl hanfodol sydd gan ymwelwyr iechyd wrth gefnogi babanod, plant a theuluoedd ledled Cymru. Yn aml, mae eu gwaith yn cael ei wneud gyda rhai o'r teuluoedd mwyaf agored i niwed yn ein cymunedau, ac maen nhw'n gwneud cyfraniad amhrisiadwy i wella canlyniadau a lleihau anghydraddoldeb.

Dwi hefyd eisiau cydnabod yr effaith mae'r anghydfod parhaus yma wedi'i chael ar yr ymwelwyr iechyd eu hunain, ar deuluoedd sy'n dibynnu ar y gwasanaethau ac ar gydweithwyr sy'n gweithio ar draws y system iechyd a gofal ehangach. Dwi'n gwybod na fyddai'r penderfyniad i streicio wedi bod yn benderfyniad hawdd iddyn nhw. Mae'r Llywodraeth yn deall cryfder y teimladau ynglŷn â'r mater yma a'r pryder sydd wedi'i fynegi gan Aelodau ar draws y Siambr.

Er hynny, mae'n bwysig bod y ddadl yma yn cael ei seilio ar ffeithiau. Wnaeth yr anghydfod hwn ddim codi dros nos. Mae'n rhagflaeni'r Llywodraeth bresennol ac mae'n fater sydd wedi bod yn mynd ymlaen ers sawl blwyddyn. Wrth wraidd yr anghydfod mae anghytundeb rhwng Unite a Bwrdd Iechyd Prifysgol Cwm Taf Morgannwg ynglŷn â gwerthuso rolau ymwelwyr iechyd a'r trefniadau band cyflog priodol.

The Government amendment reflects the reality that this remains a local employment dispute between the health board as employer and Unite as the recognised trade union, and, as such, these matters must be resolved through the established employer, trade union and industrial relations processes.

That doesn't mean that the Welsh Government has been inactive. I've engaged directly with both Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board and Unite since coming into Government and have repeatedly called on all parties to come together, engage constructively and work towards a resolution as quickly as possible. My focus has consistently been on minimising the impact on babies, families and staff, and from the outset I've placed clear expectations on Cwm Taf Morgannwg to bring forward credible solutions to this dispute. Andrew.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for that, Minister. One thing that seems to be disputed here is that, on the health board side, they seem to say that it hasn't been through an independent evaluation process, the banding from six to seven. The union says it has gone through an independent evaluation process that is recognised by the 'Agenda for Change' pay scale. Is it the Government's view that that independent evaluation process has been undertaken, and that the outcome—irrespective of the interpretation—is quite clear that these posts should be banded at band 7?

contributions.text_english:
It's not up to me to decide on the process that the health board has taken. This is an issue for the health board to resolve. They created this situation, Unite are in dispute, and they now have to come together. That's the situation we're in. It's not up to me to resolve in that respect.

So, I have sought and received detailed assurances from the chair of the health board regarding the management of risks arising from the industrial action, including safeguarding arrangements and service resilience. The Welsh Government continues to keep the situation under close review and hold the health board robustly to account in this respect.

While we are as frustrated as anyone that this dispute is ongoing, it is also important to acknowledge recent developments that have taken place. In the space of a few months after coming into office, this Welsh Government's pressure on Cwm Taf resulted in the health board bringing forward a financial settlement to end the dispute. This represents a significant step change compared to the prolonged state of deadlock that existed prior to the election. While the offer was rejected, it shows how we are doing what we can to ensure that this impasse comes to an end. We fully respect Unite's decision to reject this offer, and unlike Reform, who want to tear up the hard-won rights of workers at the behest of their shady, unaccountable billionaire paymasters, we also fully respect the right of the health visitors to continue industrial action.

While the offer was ultimately rejected, I believe it represented an important step forward in the process of bringing this long-running dispute to a satisfactory conclusion. But this can only be achieved if both parties come around the table and talk. We continue to encourage both parties to engage constructively to achieve a resolution that supports children, families and staff. I would also urge both sides to engage in good faith on derogations and actions that could be taken during this dispute, so that critical services can still be provided during the period of industrial action.

Measures are also in place to mitigate the impact of the health visitors on strike. I've said it before and I'll say it again: nobody goes on strike for fun. It's not a decision that anyone takes lightly. Collective action demands their collective support, which is what Unite are doing in supporting their members during this period. And for that, I thank them for ensuring that the health visitors are supported during a difficult time.

contributions.text_english:
As well as responding to the situation as it is, we must also consider the future of health visitor services. The Welsh Government remains fully committed to maintaining a secure and sustainable health visitor workforce across Wales. That's why the Chief Nursing Officer for Wales has commissioned work to review and consider the way in which health visitor services and wider arrangements for the workforce will be organised in the future, ensuring that they continue to meet the needs of children, families and communities in the years to come.

Llywydd, every single Member of this Senedd wants to see this dispute come to an end. We all want children and families to get the support that they need, and we want staff to feel that they are valued and supported. For those reasons, I encourage Members to support the Government's amendment that reflects the reality of the dispute and the steps that the Government has taken to encourage a solution, while continuing to protect services and support the future of the health visitor service in Wales. Thank you.
